verdicts.dateTest: The claim restated: "BlackRock, through its 50% stake in Jio BlackRock AMC, will own or control India's household savings (future tense)". Dates that fit together: the JV was announced in July 2023, got SEBI in-principle approval on 4 Oct 2024 and final approval in May 2025, and the NFO opened on 30 Jun 2025 and closed on 2 Jul 2025. BS reported it on 7 Jul 2025. The DSP exit was announced on 7 May 2018, so it came before the JV and there is no chronology conflict. The ~0.25% figure uses the Rs 17,800 cr NFO against an industry total of ~Rs 70-74 lakh crore (AMFI June 2025: Rs 74.41 lakh crore, which gives ~0.24%). That still holds. Reporting from mid-2026 puts Jio BlackRock at roughly Rs 16,700-18,000 cr against an industry of about Rs 80 lakh crore, so its share is about 0.2%. One outlier report says ~Rs 50,000 cr, which would still be under 1%. The 10% threshold in whatWouldChangeThis has not been reached.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity is Jio BlackRock Asset Management Pvt Ltd. The source says it is "a 50:50 joint venture between Jio Financial Services (JFS) and BlackRock". The DSP entity is DSP BlackRock Investment Managers. Reuters via BS, 7 May 2018: "BlackRock Inc on Monday agreed to sell its 40 percent interest in DSP BlackRock... because it could not integrate DSP BlackRock onto its technology and operating platform since it was a minority stakeholder." The actor is the same in both records (BlackRock Inc). No identity conflation.
verdicts.baseRate: Having a foreign sponsor is not unusual among Indian AMCs. Nippon Life (Japan) holds ~72% of Nippon India AMC, with ~Rs 6 lakh crore AUM and ~8% share. Amundi holds ~37% of SBI Funds Management. Prudential plc holds ~49% of ICICI Prudential AMC. Mirae, Franklin Templeton, Invesco, HSBC and others fully own their Indian AMCs. Each of these foreign sponsors has a much bigger AUM share than Jio BlackRock. The same "will control household savings" reading applied to them would have to come first, and it is not what circulates. BlackRock's 50% of a ~0.2-0.25%-share AMC does not stand out on this measure. The SPEC control set (Vanguard, NBIM, GIC, Capital Group, Fidelity, LIC) is for portfolio holdings, not AMC sponsorship. LIC MF is the domestic analogue, and it too manages a small share.
verdicts.denialFound: None found for the "control household savings" narrative itself. Nobody put this narrative to BlackRock or JFS, and it is a circulating claim, not an allegation made by a named party. The on-record BlackRock statement is from the 2018 DSP exit (spokesperson Anthony Arthur: "India remains a strategic market for BlackRock globally"), quoted in https://www.business-standard.com/article/reuters/blackrock-exits-mutual-fund-venture-with-dsp-group-118050701042_1.html. The JV's own release credits the NFO to "over 90 institutional investors" and "over 67,000 retail investors".
verdicts.innocentReading: A new 50:50 JV AMC starts the usual way, with cash and debt NFOs that corporate treasuries fill for cash management. Under the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations 1996, scheme assets belong to unit-holders. The trustee holds them through a custodian, and the AMC only manages them for a fee. BlackRock's economic interest is half of the AMC's fee income, not the assets. At ~0.2-0.25% of industry AUM, among 47 AMCs and behind much larger foreign-sponsored AMCs, this is ordinary market entry.
verdicts.reason: The narrative is stored as a speculative status with its strongest case and strongest counter, and the evidence supports that calibration. The BS 7 Jul 2025 source confirms the core facts. Quotes: "garnered ₹17,800 crore", "overnight, liquid and money market", "47-player industry", "over 90 institutional investors", "over 67,000 retail investors", "50:50 joint venture between Jio Financial Services (JFS) and BlackRock". The second BS/Reuters source confirms the 2018 DSP exit at 40% for minority-stake reasons. AUM data from 2026 shows the share has not grown meaningfully. Four details are wrong or unsupported by the sources, but none of them overturns the status. (1) "Rs 70 trillion" is not in either source; AMFI June 2025 gives Rs 74.41 lakh crore. (2) "47 other players" is wrong; the source says a 47-player industry, so 46 others. (3) The source gives investor counts, not a money split, so "institutions... supplied most of the debut money" is an inference. It is plausible for liquid/overnight funds but unsourced. (4) "AMC holds assets in trust" is legally imprecise, because the trustee/custodian holds them and the AMC manages them. Analytic is the right tier: it is our own inference, and it asserts no wrongdoing.
verdicts.corrections:
Suggested text fixes (text field and strongestCounter):
- Change "47 other players" to "46 other AMCs (47-player industry per BS)".
- Change "Rs 70-trillion industry" to "~Rs 74.4 lakh crore industry (AMFI, June 2025)" and add the AMFI monthly note as a src: https://www.amfiindia.com/Themes/Theme1/downloads/AMFIMonthlyNote_June2025.pdf
- Change "90-plus institutional investors, not households, supplied most of the debut money" to "the NFO drew 90+ institutional and 67,000+ retail investors; the institution/retail money split is undisclosed; cash/debt NFOs are typically treasury-driven (inference)".
- Change "AMC holds assets in trust" to "scheme assets are held by the trustee via a custodian for unit-holders; the AMC manages them for a fee (SEBI MF Regulations 1996)".

Other additions:
- Add an explicit innocentReading field, which CONTRACT requires for analytic.
- Add the symmetry control: Nippon Life ~72% of Nippon India AMC, Amundi ~37% of SBI MF, Prudential ~49% of ICICI Pru AMC, all with far larger AUM share.
- Add a current-status note: 2026 reporting puts Jio BlackRock at ~Rs 16,700-18,000 cr AUM, about 0.2% share. Recheck against the AMFI AMC-wise AUM table.
- Narrative srcs[1] (the 2018 Reuters/BS DSP-exit story) is not in the claim's srcs list; add it there.

verdicts.dateTest: The debunked claim is that Rothschild & Co advised Holcim or Adani on the Ambuja/ACC sale, signed 15 May 2022 and completed 16–20 Sep 2022. The sources fall in that window. The PWP transactions page lists "May 2022 CHF 6.4B". The Holcim release is dated 15 May 2022 and the Latham note 20 Sep 2022. No dates are wrong.
verdicts.identityTest: The parties are named correctly: Holcim Ltd as seller and Endeavour Trade and Investment Ltd (Adani family SPV) as BidCo. PWP says: "Financial advisor to Holcim Ltd. in connection with the sale of its 63.1% stake in Ambuja Cements Limited and 4.5% stake in ACC Limited to Adani Group". Latham says it "advised The Adani Family, through Endeavor Trade and Investment Ltd ... in the US$4.5 billion financing and successful completion of the acquisition". "Rothschild" is correctly treated as the institution Rothschild & Co (SPEC rule 1), not a family.
verdicts.baseRate: Rothschild & Co does not appear in any roster I found. Named advisers on the Holcim side: BNP Paribas, JPMorgan, Perella Weinberg (Bloomberg via Gulf News) and Freshfields as counsel. On the Adani side: Barclays and Deutsche Bank as M&A advisors, Standard Chartered as structuring advisor, ICICI Securities and Deutsche as open-offer merchant bankers, and Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas and Latham as counsel. Symmetry across the SPEC control set: JPMorgan is named (Holcim side), while Lazard, Goldman, Morgan Stanley, Citi (as adviser; it was only a lender), Kotak, Axis and Avendus are no more named than Rothschild. So the lens gives the same result for the controls: an adviser is recorded only when it is named, and the one named control (JPMorgan) is recorded.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. The narrative is being debunked, so no party has anything to deny. Neither Rothschild & Co nor Holcim was asked. No source names Rothschild in any capacity. Holcim's 15 May 2022 release names no advisers at all.
verdicts.innocentReading: The narrative likely comes from a heuristic: Holcim is Swiss, Rothschild & Co is a large European independent adviser, and Rothschild is a common target for "Rothschilds control X" narratives. The deal record simply shows other banks.
verdicts.reason: The debunk holds, and the evidence for it is stronger than the record cites. Adani's own completion release (adani.com, "Adani Becomes India's Second Largest Cement Player") lists every adviser on the buyer side: "Barclays Bank PLC and Deutsche Bank AG acted as M&A advisors to BidCo, with Standard Chartered Bank acting as the Structuring Advisor, and ICICI Securities and Deutsche Bank AG acted as merchant bankers to the open offer". Rothschild is not named. On the seller side, Bloomberg (republished by Gulf News) says: "Holcim led the transaction with its internal deal team supported by BNP Paribas SA, JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Perella Weinberg Partners." PWP's page confirms its role. The record is only partially sourced, though. (1) It implies Perella Weinberg was Holcim's sole adviser; PWP's page does not say "exclusive", and BNP Paribas and JPMorgan were co-advisers. (2) "Neither Holcim's nor Adani's release names Rothschild" is trivially true for Holcim, because that release names no advisers at all. The Adani release that does list advisers is not cited. (3) Latham is legal counsel, not a financial adviser, so it is weak evidence against a financial-adviser claim. The analytic tier fits, because the conclusion is an inference from absence across the complete disclosed rosters.
verdicts.corrections: text: change to "Rothschild advised Holcim or Adani on the 2022 Ambuja/ACC sale — status: debunked (Holcim was advised by BNP Paribas, JPMorgan and Perella Weinberg; Adani's BidCo by Barclays and Deutsche Bank (M&A), Standard Chartered (structuring) and ICICI Securities/Deutsche (open offer); no party names Rothschild)". strongestCounter: replace "Perella Weinberg's own transaction record states it was financial adviser to Holcim" with the full seller-side list (BNP Paribas, JPMorgan, PWP). Also replace "neither Holcim's nor Adani's release names Rothschild" with "Adani's 20 Sep 2022 completion release lists all buyer-side advisers and omits Rothschild; Holcim's 15 May 2022 release names no advisers". srcs: add https://www.adani.com/newsroom/media-releases/adani-becomes-indias-second-largest-cement-player (primary adviser roster) and https://gulfnews.com/business/gautam-adani-asias-richest-man-forges-105-billion-deal-with-holcim-1.87894359 (Bloomberg: Holcim advisers). Optionally add https://www.freshfields.us/news/2022/05/freshfields-advises-holcim-on-the-sale-of-indian-business-to-adani-group/ (Holcim counsel). Relabel Latham as "legal counsel on financing and acquisition", not financial adviser. Keep tier analytic, with innocentReading as above.

verdicts.dateTest: The facts are in date order. Deloitte quoted Re 1 for the BPCL transaction-adviser (TA) mandate, with presentations to DIPAM on 28 Nov 2019 and the BS report on 4 Dec 2019. The BPCL sale was called off on 26 May 2022 (DIPAM archive, c003), so it never closed. KPMG won the IDBI Bank TA mandate for Re 1 (BS, 26/27 Aug 2021). As of 25 Sep 2026, IDBI had not closed either: BS reports 'Govt evaluating financial bids for strategic stake sale in IDBI Bank' (https://www.business-standard.com/amp/companies/news/govt-evaluating-financial-bids-for-strategic-stake-sale-in-idbi-bank-126092500411_1.html), with Fairfax and Emirates NBD revised bids in July 2026. 'Neither sale closed' is true on the file's asOf date of 2026-09-26. One caveat: the IDBI stake on sale is now 60.72% (GoI 30.48% + LIC 30.24%), which is not the 45.48% in the 2021 article.
verdicts.identityTest: Both entities match the sources. BS 2019 names 'Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu India' (the same entity as DTTILLP in the DIPAM BPCL EoI). BS 2021 names 'KPMG India' and lists the seven bidders by legal name. SBI Caps was the losing state-owned bidder in both processes. Two identity problems in the counter-case: the JM Financial Re 1 was for ONGC's purchase of HPCL, a mandate given by ONGC and not a DIPAM selection. And Citi on Coal India is described as having 'quoted a very low share', not Re 1.
verdicts.baseRate: This is non-discriminating. Per the file's own baseRates, Big Four firms won 5 of 7 DIPAM TA mandates with an opened source (71%). The fee is known for only 2 of 7, and both are Re 1, so there is no fee distribution to compare against. Symmetry fails for the 'Big Four' framing. BS names the same near-zero practice for non-Big Four firms: Citi on the 2010 Coal India IPO, where all bidders 'had to match it', and JM Financial's Rs 1 on ONGC-HPCL. KPMG beat six bidders at IDBI, including non-Big Four ICICI Securities, JM Financial, RBSA and SBI Caps. The property is a feature of the lowest-fee selection rule, not of the Big Four.
verdicts.denialFound: No firm denies a quid pro quo because no named party alleges one. My search found no politician, petition, CAG or Parliament finding that makes the charge in India. On the fees: 'Both Deloitte and SBI Caps did not respond to emailed queries' (BS 4 Dec 2019). KPMG: 'DIPAM is running the process for selecting a transaction advisor. Hence we would refrain from commenting on the ongoing process' (BS 26 Aug 2021). So both firms were asked about the fee; neither was asked about a quid pro quo.
verdicts.innocentReading: The fee is ranked lowest-wins among technically qualified bidders, so a token Re 1 bid wins a flagship mandate. The firms accept it as a loss leader to build credentials. Both sources say this directly. BPCL: 'For Deloitte, this may be a prestigious deal and will add to its portfolio a national energy company'. Former CIL chairman Partha Bhattacharya: Deloitte 'could have gone for a notional token figure to get their name associated with this'. IDBI: 'The near-zero bid could make KPMG one of the largest players in managing deals in the financial services space'. BS also says 'Firms have been placing near-zero bids ... as a means to improve their portfolios and establish credentials'.
verdicts.reason: Both BS sources say exactly what the factual parts claim. Quotes: 'Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu India has quoted Rs 1 to manage the sale of Bharat Petroleum Corporation' (SBI Caps second-lowest at Rs 15-17 crore) and 'KPMG placed the lowest bid of Re 1, and was selected as the transaction adviser, said an official'. Neither source says or implies a quid pro quo. Both give credential-building as the motive. The record is a narrative held at analytic tier with a strongest counter, and it asserts no wrongdoing, so it survives at analytic. What it cannot support is the status 'contested': nothing on the record supports the quid pro quo side. The only pro-thesis item beyond the two Re 1 wins, 'the same firms hold large government consulting books', has no source. The 'two documented Re 1 wins' wording also overstates the evidence. Each Re 1 fee rests on one outlet citing unnamed people ('three persons in the know'; 'an official'), which the file itself tiers as reported (c004, c009). The appointments are documented; the fees are not.
verdicts.corrections:
1. text: change 'two documented Re 1 wins' to 'two reported Re 1 wins (single outlet, unnamed sources; Deloitte's BPCL appointment is documented by DIPAM's EoI, but no fee is documented)'.
2. status: change 'contested' to 'not supported'. No named party alleges a quid pro quo, and no source offers evidence for it.
3. strongestCase: either source 'the same firms hold large government consulting books' with a primary record (for example, GeM/CPPP awards or a Parliament answer) or delete it. It is currently unsourced.
4. 'no follow-on reward documented': rewrite to 'the file records later DIPAM/MoF mandates to Deloitte (CONCOR TA Dec 2019, reportedly also near-Re 1; LIC pre-IPO Sep 2020, from a June 2020 tender). Both were competitive awards, not rewards, and no non-competitive follow-on is documented.' The current wording hides entries c005 and c010 in the same file.
5. strongestCounter: the lowest-fee (L1) rule is our inference. BS describes Coal India as others 'had to match' Citi's low quote. ONGC-HPCL was an ONGC mandate, not a DIPAM one. Citi's Coal India quote was 'very low', not Re 1.
6. Add a symmetry note: near-zero bids by Citi and JM Financial show the practice is not specific to the Big Four.
7. Update IDBI: not closed as of BS 25 Sep 2026 (financial bids under evaluation, 60.72% stake), and add that URL.
8. Add killIf/upgradeIf per the existing whatWouldChangeThis.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim written out: BlackRock and Vanguard own India's listed companies, now. Holdings windows: HDFC Bank SHP quarter ended 30.06.2026 (opened, current). ITC and Bharti Airtel are 31.12.2025. SBI is 31.03.2025, which is stale by five quarters. The Jio BlackRock NFO was July 2025. BIS CGFS 66 is dated 13 May 2021, five years before the holdings and industry-wide rather than India-specific. The windows overlap closely enough for a present-tense calibration. The only real date weakness is SBI's quarter.
verdicts.identityTest: HDFC Bank's primary SHP (opened) names 'VANGUARD TOTAL INTERNATIONAL STOCK INDEX FUND' (PAN AABTV0442N) at 1.25% and 'VANGUARD EMERGING MARKETS STOCK INDEX FUND, A SERIES OF VANGUARD INTERNATIONAL EQUITY INDEX FUNDS' (AAATY0918K) at 1.19%, which sum to the 2.44% in the record. Confirmed. These are separately registered FPI fund vehicles, not 'Vanguard Group' as one holder. Bharti Airtel's SHP (opened) shows 'PASTEL LIMITED ... Promoter Group ... 7.49%'. Confirmed, and no BlackRock, iShares or Vanguard line appears. Pastel is Singtel's vehicle, but Singtel also co-owns Bharti Telecom Ltd, the promoter at 40.47%. So '7.49%' understates Singtel's strategic position, which makes the counter stronger. BlackRock is correctly kept apart from Jio BlackRock AMC, a 50:50 JV that owns no listed operating companies.
verdicts.baseRate: Index funds from both managers hold essentially every NIFTY 50 constituent, so 'held by BlackRock/Vanguard' is about 100% and tells you nothing. At the named ≥1% level across all 17 primary filings the capital fleet opened (holders.json 5, b1 3, b2 1, b3 3, b4 3, b6 2): BlackRock is named in 0 of 17. Vanguard is named in 4 of 17 (HDFC Bank 2.44%, Axis Bank, Cipla 1.01%, M&M 2.14% across two funds), always as two index-fund lines of about 1% each, never ≥5%, and never with a board seat or promoter classification. Controls under the same lens: GIC/Singapore and NBIM cross 1% about as often or more often. LIC crosses in most filings and is Axis Bank's promoter. Strategic FDI and promoter vehicles (BAT 22.91% of ITC, Suzuki at Maruti, Pastel/Bharti Telecom, the Adani offshore promoter cluster) are much larger than any passive line. Rough sizing (analytic, unsourced): both managers' combined India equity exposure is probably around 1–2% of market cap.
verdicts.denialFound: none found. Not asked. Neither BlackRock nor Vanguard was asked about the India-specific narrative, and no India-specific statement was located. Their generic position that the assets belong to fund clients was not retrieved or verified here, so none is recorded.
verdicts.innocentReading: Global cap-weighted index funds (Vanguard Total International and EM Index, iShares) hold every large Indian stock in proportion to index weight for their clients' benefit. Where one fund's line crosses the SEBI 1% naming threshold, that reflects the stock's index weight, not an attempt to control it. Voting follows stewardship policy. Control in Indian companies sits with promoters, the state (the President of India holds 57.43% of SBI) and strategic FDI holders.
verdicts.reason: I could not refute the record. Its verdict, 'unsupported', rests on evidence I checked. Primary shareholding filings (I opened HDFC Bank's and Bharti Airtel's) confirm Vanguard at 2.44% of HDFC Bank split across two index funds, Pastel at 7.49% of Bharti Airtel, and no BlackRock/iShares line. Across all 17 primary filings the fleet opened, BlackRock is named in none and Vanguard only as roughly 1% index lines. The symmetry control goes against the narrative: the same lens picks out GIC, NBIM and above all LIC more often than BlackRock. The record rightly stops short of 'debunked'. The SEBI ≥1% naming threshold is per registered vehicle, so a zero named-holder count cannot rule out a larger aggregate, and it records that falsifier honestly. The claim itself is not something the platform asserts. It is a narrative, and the calibration is our own inference, so 'analytic' with an innocent reading is the right tier. It does not frame a family, religion or ethnicity as the actor. Several details need fixing (below), but none of them changes the verdict.
verdicts.corrections: 1) strongestCounter: '0 of 5 ... 45 constituents remain unchecked' is stale. Change it to 'BlackRock named ≥1% in 0 of 17 primary filings opened across holders.json and holders-b1–b6; Vanguard in 4 of 17 (HDFC Bank, Axis Bank, Cipla, Mahindra & Mahindra); about 33 constituents unchecked at named-holder level.' 2) 'LIC is the largest non-promoter holder in 3 of 5' is only true if Bharti Airtel counts through a LIC ULIP fund line (3.81%, not LIC's direct book). The source says 'In many countries, portfolio investors have surpassed banks as the largest source of foreign credit.' Quote that instead. 5) Change the src URL https://www.bis.org/publ/cgfs66.pdf, which now redirects to a landing page, to https://www.bis.org/publications/cgfs-paper-66-changing-patterns-capital-flows (13 May 2021). Add the holders.json primary SHP URLs (HDFC Bank June 2026, Bharti Airtel Dec 2025) to srcs, since the counter rests on them, not on BIS. 6) The SBI figure is from the quarter ended 31.03.2025. Refresh it or date it. 7) Add denial: 'none found — not asked'.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: "The Rothschild family (actor) controls (did) the RBI and Indian banking (thing), now (when)." The RBI's own About Us page says it was "established on April 1, 1935 in accordance with the provisions of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934" and that "since nationalisation in 1949, the Reserve Bank is fully owned by the Government of India". Rothschild & Co India Pvt Ltd was incorporated in 1998 (CIN U65990MH1998PTC116788). So since 1949 the State has owned 100% of the RBI, and the Rothschild entity only appears 49 years later, as an adviser. The two windows have no ownership or control overlap. The 1935-49 shareholder period is not claimed or evidenced in any source. Ferguson's period of Rothschild dominance, 1820s-1870s (as quoted on Wikipedia), ended before the RBI existed. The date test supports the debunk.
verdicts.identityTest: The claim names a family as the actor, which the project rules do not allow as an actor. The file correctly swaps in the institutional referent. That referent checks out: the India page names "Rothschild & Co India Private Limited", CIN U65990MH1998PTC116788, SEBI Category-I Merchant Banker INM000010668. Its listed services are M&A and strategic advisory, fundraising and strategic capital, financing advisory, and restructuring. It lists no banking, lending or deposit-taking. The RBI's board "is appointed by the Government of India in keeping with the Reserve Bank of India Act". Two identity defects: (1) the strongestCase says "SEBI merchant banker since 1998", but the source gives only the 1998 CIN and the registration number, not a SEBI registration date. (2) The PRH source is Ferguson Vol. 1, "Money's Prophets: 1798-1848". The "1820s-1870s" dominance quote comes from Wikipedia, not from the PRH page.
verdicts.baseRate: The RBI is 100% owned by the Government of India. The foreign-adviser control set in the SPEC (Rothschild & Co, Lazard, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, JP Morgan, Citi) therefore shares the property "has no ownership or board role in the RBI" at a 100% rate. No named ≥1% holding in the bank SHPs opened by holders.json is also near 100% for the set. Absence does not single out Rothschild. It is simply the default for every foreign advisory firm. Symmetry: the same lens applied to Lazard, the SPEC control, gives the same reading (adviser, no control). It would reject "Goldman/BlackRock controls the RBI" in exactly the same way.
verdicts.denialFound: None found. Not asked. The narrative accuses no documented act by Rothschild & Co, so no specific response exists. The firm's India page describes its business as advisory only (https://www.rothschildandco.com/en/countries/india/). The RBI's own statement of 100% government ownership (https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/AboutusDisplay.aspx) is the institutional record that answers the claim.
verdicts.innocentReading: Rothschild & Co runs a Mumbai advisory team of about 30 bankers. It earns deal fees (145 M&A deals since 2010 by its own count), takes occasional high-profile mandates, and carries a famous 19th-century name. That fully explains why the name comes up in Indian finance. The central bank is state-owned under a 1934 statute. Its board is appointed by the government. Indian bank equity is held mainly by the State, LIC, domestic funds and fragmented FPIs.
verdicts.reason:
The "debunked" verdict survives. The load-bearing counter is a primary record: the RBI's own page says it has been "fully owned by the Government of India" since 1949 and that its board "is appointed by the Government of India in keeping with the Reserve Bank of India Act". Rothschild & Co's India page lists only advisory and fundraising services under a SEBI merchant-banker registration. The Wikipedia source supports the antisemitic-trope classification, the fictional Waterloo profiteering story ("That he used the news for financial advantage was a fiction") and the Nazi propaganda use (Der ewige Jude; Die Rothschilds, 1940). As an edge, "Rothschild family → controls RBI" must be killed: a family is not an actor. It survives only as a narrative with status debunked. The supporting prose has defects that need fixing:
(a) Dairnvaell's 1846 pamphlet appears in none of the four cited sources. I grepped the full Wikipedia Rothschild_family wikitext: no "Dairnvaell" and no "1846".
(b) "SEBI merchant banker since 1998" is not in the source.
(c) The strongestCase leaves out the strongest real links, which weakens the steelman:
  - The NSE appointed Rothschild & Co as independent adviser for its IPO on 12 Feb 2026 (Reuters via MarketScreener: "The National Stock Exchange of India on Thursday said that it has appointed Rothschild & Co as an independent advisor to oversee its long-awaited initial public offering"). This is not recorded anywhere in research/raw/capital.
  - DIPAM chose Rothschild as Air India transaction adviser in Oct 2017 before it withdrew (BS, 28 Oct / 14 Nov 2017, already flagged in AUDIT.json for narrative:0).
Both are mandates, not control, so the verdict does not change.

2. strongestCase: add "NSE appointed Rothschild & Co independent adviser for its IPO, 12 Feb 2026 (Reuters, https://www.marketscreener.com/news/india-s-nse-appoints-rothschild-as-independent-advisor-for-ipo-ce7e5ad2d188f42c; BS https://www.business-standard.com/markets/news/nse-appoints-rothschild-co-as-independent-adviser-for-ipo-process-126021201509_1.html)". Also add "chosen as Air India transaction adviser by DIPAM, Oct 2017, then withdrew over the 0.2% fee (Business Standard)". Add the sources to srcs and note that these are advisory mandates, not ownership or control.
3. strongestCounter: either add a source for "Dairnvaell's 1846 pamphlet" (e.g. Ferguson, The House of Rothschild Vol. 1, which covers 1798-1848 and the Waterloo legend, with page cited) or delete it. None of the four srcs mention it.

6. strongestCounter: qualify "absent from every named-holder filing" as "absent as a named >1% holder in the five NIFTY 50 SHPs opened in holders.json (SEBI SHPs name only >1% holders)".
7. Graph: record no edge from any Rothschild node to the RBI or to any bank. Any family-as-actor edge is kill. Keep the item only as narrative status "debunked".

verdicts.dateTest: Written as a claim: Soros/OSF, Hindenburg and OCCRP coordinated a campaign against Adani and Modi, Jan 2023 to Dec 2024. The dated events all hold. Hindenburg's report is dated 24 Jan 2023 and says "we have taken a short position in Adani Group Companies through U.S.-traded bonds and non-Indian-traded derivative instruments". Soros spoke at Munich on 16 Feb 2023 (Al Jazeera). The record says "16–17 Feb", but 17 Feb was the date of Smriti Irani's reply. OCCRP, the Guardian and the FT published on 31 Aug 2023, about seven months after Hindenburg. The Supreme Court ruled on 3 Jan 2024 (para 40: reliance on "reports by third-party organizations ... does not inspire confidence"). The Hindenburg SEBI-chair report is dated 10 Aug 2024. Drop Site published on 2 Dec 2024. The Lokpal order is dated 28 May 2025. The SEBI WTM order is dated 18 Sep 2025 ("the allegations made against Noticees in the SCN are not established ... dispose of the instant proceedings ... without any direction"). No date conflicts with the record. The order of events actually works against coordination: OCCRP says it built on funds Hindenburg had already named but "did not reveal who was using them", which looks like follow-up reporting, not a joint launch.
verdicts.identityTest: The accused are identified correctly: Open Society Foundations as an institution, Hindenburg Research (Nathan Anderson), and OCCRP (a 501(c)(3)). This is an individual plus institutions, not a family, religion or ethnicity, so it can stay a narrative. Because the "Soros" framing often carries antisemitic undertones, it must never become a 'coordination' edge. One identity fact is missing from the record. The only documented party with money in Hindenburg's Adani trade is Kingdon Capital Management (Mark Kingdon), not Soros or OSF. SEBI's show-cause notice (27 Jun 2024, reported 2 Jul 2024) says Hindenburg "colluded with its client Kingdon Capital Management by providing a draft of its report", and Kingdon shorted through K India Opportunities Fund (a Kotak Mahindra International fund). Hindenburg said it earned "$4.1m in gross revenue ... from that investor relationship" and "$31,000" from its own bond short (Al Jazeera, 2 Jul 2024). So "Hindenburg's investors are undisclosed" is only partly true. Its equity investors are undisclosed, but its documented trading counterparty is named, and it is not Soros.
verdicts.baseRate: OCCRP's funders page, as fetched on 26 Sep 2026, lists 25 institutional donors, including the US State Department, UK FCDO, Sida, the Dutch Foreign Ministry, MacArthur and Skoll. OSF is only one of them. Sullivan says OCCRP has "more than 40 donors", and Business Standard counted 21 on the page in Sep 2023. Nearly every major investigative network (OCCRP, ICIJ, Forbidden Stories) takes money from OSF and/or Western governments. "Takes OSF money and published about a big conglomerate" is therefore close to universal among such outlets (well over 80%), so it doesn't single anyone out. Many parties also shared interest in Adani after Jan 2023: short sellers, FT, Reuters, Bloomberg, and India's opposition. Shared interest and a shared political reading of a market collapse are normal. The mirror test is in the file's own symmetryCheck (3). The 12 Aug 2024 defence of Buch by AMFI, Adani, BJP figures and the then IMF executive director within 48 hours, carried by the state broadcaster, looks equally 'coordinated' under the same test. So the test says nothing about either side.
verdicts.denialFound: Yes, and the record leaves it out. OSF told CNN (1 Sep 2023) that it is "proud to be amongst a number of organizations providing general support to the OCCRP which acts entirely independently regarding the issues it chooses to investigate. What we are seeing now in India is a bogus attempt to discredit OCCRP's work without engaging with its findings." https://www.cnn.com/2023/09/01/business/adani-soros-india/index.html. OCCRP (Sullivan on X, same CNN piece): all donors have signed agreements "giving total editorial control to the network". OCCRP to ThePrint (Dec 2024): the US has "no say in our editorial processes" (already recorded as c021). OSF, Sep 2023 (Al Jazeera, 26 Dec 2024): its India grant-making has been "constrained by government restrictions" since mid-2016. Hindenburg: no statement located on a Soros link. It called SEBI's show-cause notice "nonsense" and "concocted to serve a pre-ordained purpose". Also missing is the named source of the narrative itself. Adani Group, 31 Aug 2023 (adani.com media statement): "These news reports appear to be yet another concerted bid by Soros-funded interests supported by a section of the foreign media to revive the meritless Hindenburg report." https://www.adani.com/newsroom/media-releases/media-statement-on-a-report
verdicts.innocentReading: Hindenburg is a for-profit short seller. It researched Adani, gave a draft to a paying hedge-fund client (Kingdon), and made money on the fall; the documented motive is profit, not politics. OCCRP is a donor-funded investigative network, and OSF says it gives about 4% of OCCRP's funding. OCCRP followed up on the Mauritius funds Hindenburg had named but couldn't attribute, and published seven months later with the Guardian and FT from bank and tax-haven documents. Soros, a known long-time Modi critic, commented publicly on a big market event, as many commentators did. Three actors with different motives (profit, journalism, ideology) converged on the most-covered corporate story in India. No communication, payment or instruction links them.
verdicts.reason: The "unsupported" status holds. Every source I opened confirms the individual parts, and none shows a link between Soros/OSF and Hindenburg, or any direction or coordination among the three. The only documented money relationship in Hindenburg's Adani trade is with Kingdon Capital (per SEBI's show-cause notice and Hindenburg's own disclosure), which cuts against the Soros link. The symmetry test on the Aug 2024 pro-Buch statements gives an equally 'coordinated' picture. The coordination claim itself is best tiered as alleged: named parties assert it (Adani Group 31 Aug 2023, Smriti Irani 17 Feb 2023, Sambit Patra 7 Dec 2024), and denials exist (OSF, OCCRP). The record does have factual errors and gaps, listed in the corrections. The biggest are that the one-line text says "common funder documented" when no funder shared by any two of the three accused is documented, and that OSF's share of OCCRP funding is not "unpublished": OCCRP says 4%.
verdicts.corrections:
1. Claim text: replace "common funder documented" with "OSF funding of OCCRP documented (OCCRP-stated ~4%, Sep 2023); no funder shared by any two of the three documented; coordination and any Soros→Hindenburg link undocumented".
2. strongestCounter: replace "OSF is one of 26 OCCRP funders with an unpublished share" with "OSF is one of 25 institutional donors on OCCRP's page (fetched 26 Sep 2026; 21 in Sep 2023 per Business Standard; OCCRP says >40 donors in total); OCCRP says OSF supplies 4% of its funding (CNN, 1 Sep 2023)". Add CNN https://www.cnn.com/2023/09/01/business/adani-soros-india/index.html to srcs.
3. strongestCase (2): change "at Munich on 16–17 Feb 2023" to "at Munich on 16 Feb 2023 (BJP reply 17 Feb)".
4. strongestCounter: change "Hindenburg's investors are undisclosed" to "Hindenburg's equity investors are undisclosed; its documented trading counterparty on Adani is Kingdon Capital Management, to which SEBI's 27 Jun 2024 show-cause notice alleges a draft was supplied (K India Opportunities Fund, ~Rs 183 crore profit), with Hindenburg reporting US$4.1m gross from that relationship". Add sources Al Jazeera 2 Jul 2024 https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2024/7/2/new-twist-in-clash-between-us-short-seller-hindenburg-and-indias-adani and Business Standard 2 Jul 2024.
5. Name who makes the claim. Add to strongestCase, and as an alleged edge grp:adani → cap:open-society-foundations, the Adani Group statement of 31 Aug 2023: "yet another concerted bid by Soros-funded interests supported by a section of the foreign media to revive the meritless Hindenburg report" (https://www.adani.com/newsroom/media-releases/media-statement-on-a-report). Also fix c002/c004 to quote this sentence; they currently omit it.
6. Add a contra edge cap:open-society-foundations → that claim, quoting the OSF statement to CNN of 1 Sep 2023 ("acts entirely independently ... a bogus attempt to discredit OCCRP's work without engaging with its findings").
7. c038 ("No response recorded"): note that OSF did respond on OCCRP. No Hindenburg or Soros statement on a Soros–Hindenburg link was located.
8. strongestCase (6): the Lokpal quote ends "... corner Adani Group of Companies". Quote it in full.
9. The narrative's status stays "unsupported". Tier the underlying coordination assertion "alleged", with the OSF and OCCRP contras.

verdicts.dateTest: Chronology holds. SIT on black money set up May 2014. The Rs 2.715 lakh crore ODI figure is as of end-Feb 2015 (SEBI to SIT). The India–Mauritius protocol was signed 10 May 2016 and gives source taxation from 1 Apr 2017. SEBI tightened ODIs by board decision 19 May 2016 and by circular 7 Jul 2017. Hindenburg published 24 Jan 2023, and SEBI's granular FPI look-through circular came in Aug 2023, so the sequence is right. OCCRP published 31 Aug 2023. SEBI's related-party orders are dated 18 Sep 2025, which fits the "finished strands" wording. One timing error: the 2024 protocol was signed 7 Mar 2024 but is not in force. EY: "The protocol has not yet entered into force." EY India, Jul 2026: the Mauritian Cabinet approved ratification on 17 Jul 2026, and neither side has notified completion yet. "Renegotiated ... again in 2024" needs a note that it is signed but not in force.
verdicts.identityTest: The actors are institutions (Union of India, SIT, SEBI, Mauritius FSC) and named funds (EIFF, EMRF, Excel Investment and Advisory Services). No family, religion or ethnicity is framed as the actor, so this stays a narrative and is not killed on identity grounds. Two identity slips. (1) The headline claim is about FPI money, but the key statistic is about FDI. NTU: "Between 2000 to 2015, over a third of all foreign investments into India were channelled through Mauritius." Gunputh et al.: "nearly 34% of total Foreign Direct Investment". That supports a claim about FDI routing, not FPI. (2) "Taking instructions from a Vinod Adani-linked adviser" matches OCCRP: "An agreement for Excel to provide advisory services to EIFF and EMRF was signed for Excel by Vinod Adani himself in 2011." But Vinod Adani is a non-resident (Cyprus/Dubai). The OCCRP/Hindenburg mechanism is concealed promoter holdings (minimum public shareholding and manipulation). It is not specifically "Indian black money", so "exactly this mechanism" overstates the fit.
verdicts.baseRate: Routing through a low-tax treaty jurisdiction is not a discriminating property. Before 2017, treaty shopping via Mauritius or Singapore was the rational choice for essentially every non-resident investor. Today Mauritius is a minority FPI domicile: about Rs 4.39 trillion AUC at end-June 2024, fifth behind Ireland, roughly 6% of total FPI AUC (Business Standard, 10 Jul 2024). Mauritius and Singapore together are about 25%. The SIT's own ODI data works against the "via Mauritius" specificity. Arthapedia quoting the SIT: "the top five locations of end Beneficial owner of ODIs were Cayman Islands, USA, UK, Mauritus and Bermuda contributing to 31.31%, 14.20%, 13.49%, 9.91% and 9.10%". Symmetry: the same lens flags Singapore (its protocol was amended in parallel in 2016), Cayman, Luxembourg and Ireland equally. Both governments acted on it: UPA with the 2007 ODI curbs and 2012 White Paper, NDA in 2016, 2017, 2023 and 2024. So the lens tells you about tax-haven domicile, not about Indian residency.
verdicts.denialFound: Adani Group, via OCCRP 31 Aug 2023: "these allegations are not only baseless and unsubstantiated but are rehashed from Hindenburg's allegations" (https://www.occrp.org/en/investigation/documents-provide-fresh-insight-into-allegations-of-stock-manipulation-that-rocked-indias-powerful-adani-group). Mauritius Financial Services Minister Mahen Seeruttun told the Mauritian Parliament that Hindenburg's shell-company allegations were "false and baseless". He said Mauritian law does not allow shell companies and all licensed Global Business Companies must meet substance requirements. The FSC said its initial assessment found no non-compliance by Adani-related entities (https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/nation/no-shell-company-in-mauritius-hindenburg-allegations-false-baseless-mauritius-min-tells-parliament-506572). FSC, Aug 2024: the IPE Plus funds are not FSC licensees and are not domiciled in Mauritius (https://www.business-standard.com/pti-stories/national/fsc-mauritius-says-fund-at-heart-of-hindenburg-allegations-against-sebi-chief-not-domiciled-in-mauritius-124081301930_1.html). The narrative record's strongestCounter does not include the Mauritius denial.
verdicts.innocentReading: Foreign investors used Mauritius, and later Singapore, Ireland and Luxembourg, because of zero capital-gains tax under the treaty. The routing is tax arbitrage by genuinely foreign money. The state renegotiated treaties and tightened ODI and FPI rules to close a known channel of abuse and to recover tax revenue. None of that shows that a material share of FPI assets belongs to Indian residents. The Mauritius share of FPI AUC fell after source taxation started in 2017. That fits tax-driven routing, not residency-driven routing.
verdicts.reason: The parenthetical calibration holds up against the sources. The structure (treaty shopping, SIT concern, SEBI ODI and look-through rules) is documented by primary or credible sources, and no official numerator for the round-tripped share exists. The headline claim does not hold at "contested" as a general statement about FPI money, for three reasons. (1) The only official breakdown in hand, the SIT's ODI beneficial-owner locations, puts Mauritius at 9.91%, behind Cayman, the USA and the UK. (2) Mauritius is only about 6% of FPI AUC (2024). (3) The one specific alleged instance (Adani) involves a non-resident promoter relative, and SEBI's finished strands did not establish a violation. What the record supports is that the mechanism is documented and specific instances are alleged by named parties (Hindenburg, OCCRP) and denied. It does not support "FPI money is round-tripped black money". Keep it as a narrative at alleged/unsupported-as-generalisation, with the structural elements tiered documented separately.
verdicts.corrections: 1. status: change "contested" to "unsupported as a generalisation; mechanism documented; specific instances alleged". As a claim tier use alleged, with the Adani and Mauritius FSC denials as contra. 2. strongestCase: relabel "over a third of FDI into India 2000–2015" as an FDI statistic (DIPP about 34%, Gunputh et al. 2017) and add that it says nothing about FPI composition. Add the FPI figure: Mauritius about Rs 4.39 trillion AUC, about 6%, 5th, end-June 2024 (Business Standard 10 Jul 2024, https://www.business-standard.com/markets/news/mauritius-slips-to-fifth-place-on-preferred-fpi-destinations-list-124071001004_1.html). 3. The 2024 protocol: add "signed 7 Mar 2024; not in force as of Sep 2026 (Mauritian Cabinet approved ratification 17 Jul 2026; mutual notifications pending)". 4. strongestCounter: add the SIT's ODI beneficial-owner location split quoted in Arthapedia (Cayman 31.31%, USA 14.20%, UK 13.49%, Mauritius 9.91%, Bermuda 9.10%), and add the Mauritius minister and FSC denials with URLs. 5. Soften "Hindenburg alleged exactly this mechanism for Adani" to "Hindenburg alleged Mauritius vehicles linked to Vinod Adani, a non-resident, were used to hold and trade Adani stock". That is concealed promoter holding, not necessarily resident black money. 6. Note that SEBI's FPI/MPS strand (12 FPIs, overseas information requests) was still open when last reported. Only the related-party strands were closed, on 18 Sep 2025.

verdicts.dateTest: Stated as a claim: the World Bank and IMF (actor) dictate (did) Indian economic policy (thing), with no date given (when), so it implicitly means the present. The dated facts in the record check out. P173943 is dated "April 30, 2020" with "Total Financing 750.00", which confirms US$750m on 30 Apr 2020. India's IMF borrowing matches the record: a 1981 EFF, then the 1991 facilities, the last being an upper-credit-tranche SBA approved 31 Oct 1991 (SDR 1,656m, drawn over 20 months). The RBI history says India has taken no IMF money since 1993 and finished repaying by 2000 (rbidocs.rbi.org.in Chapter12_04122018.pdf). So "no IMF programme since 1991" is right as to when programmes were approved; the last drawing was in 1993. The World Bank operations and the IMF programmes do not overlap in time with any current IMF leverage. Two things are dated wrong. "Rs 45-lakh-crore Union budget" is the FY2023-24 figure; with asOf in 2026 the Union budget is about Rs 50–53 lakh crore. And "US$2.75bn of 2020 budget support" does not match the finance file's own breakdown (see corrections).
verdicts.identityTest: The institutions are named correctly. P173943 is "Accelerating India's COVID-19 Social Protection Response Program", the first of a planned two-operation DPO series ("US$750 million and US$250 million respectively"). The 26-prior-action count across P173943, P174292 and P181032 comes from finance/worldbank.json narrative 0, not from the one source this record cites, so the record takes that count on trust. Nothing here frames a family, religion or ethnicity as the actor; the actors are institutions.
verdicts.baseRate: Development-policy lending always comes with prior actions, so every DPO borrower has "conditions". That puts the rate near 100% and makes it useless for telling dictation apart from ordinary lending. The same lens applied to any IBRD borrower, or to India's own conditional grants to states under Finance Commission and CSS terms, would also read as "dictation". Among large emerging markets, a long spell with no IMF programme (India since 1993) is unusual on the side that counts against the narrative.
verdicts.denialFound: None needed in the usual sense. The narrative makes no specific allegation against a named party. The Bank's own document describes the operation as supporting GoI's PMGKY: "The PMGKY program is not a new scheme, rather an integrated package scaling up cash and food assistance through pre-existing programs". Nobody was asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: Conditionality attached to programmes the borrower had already announced is a way to finance them, not control over them. Bank lending is small next to a Union budget of more than Rs 50 lakh crore that is mostly funded by domestically held rupee debt. The 1991 IMF conditionality came during a balance-of-payments crisis that ended by 1993–2000.
verdicts.reason: I could not refute the "unsupported" verdict. The primary source confirms the facts it is used for: US$750m, 30 Apr 2020, and financing of the already-announced PMGKY with Prior Action 1 as GoI's own approval of PMGKY. The RBI record backs the claim that India has had no IMF money since 1993. The steelman needs fixing, though. It mislabels US$2.75bn as "budget support". It also leaves out the best evidence for the narrative, which sits in this same source: the Bank writes that "Structural and policy shifts that the Bank expected to see evolve over several years have become possible today as a result of the COVID-19 crisis" and that it "partnered with GoI to respond to this important policy opening". That is Bank influence and agenda-alignment language, not dictation. An honest steelman should quote it. The verdict and the analytic tier both stand.
verdicts.corrections: 1) strongestCase: change "US$2.75bn of 2020 budget support" to "US$2.75bn of 2020 emergency commitments (health US$1bn investment project, social protection US$1.15bn, MSME US$0.75bn), of which only the DPOs (about US$1.9bn) were budget support", matching finance/worldbank.json line ~4091. 2) strongestCase: add the P173943 quote "Structural and policy shifts that the Bank expected to see evolve over several years have become possible today as a result of the COVID-19 crisis ... partnered with GoI to respond to this important policy opening". 3) strongestCounter: replace "Rs 45-lakh-crore Union budget" with the budget year in force at asOf (FY2025-26 about Rs 50.65 lakh crore, or the FY2026-27 figure) and name the FY. 4) strongestCounter: replace "no IMF programme since 1991 (... not independently re-verified)" with "last IMF arrangement: SBA approved 31 Oct 1991, SDR 1,656m; no IMF drawings since 1993, fully repaid by 2000" and cite RBI, https://rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/content/PDFs/Chapter12_04122018.pdf. 5) srcs: add the P174292 and P181032 program documents that the 26-prior-actions count depends on, or mark that count as inherited from finance/worldbank.json narrative 0. 6) Normalise the source URL to https://documents.worldbank.org/... (the documents1 http link works but redirects).

verdicts.dateTest: Restated claim: SEBI (actor) granted Jio BlackRock AMC in-principle MF approval on 4 Oct 2024 and final registration on 26 May 2025, on a JFS application of 19 Oct 2023. The dates overlap and nothing is anachronistic. I confirmed them in BS 27 May 2025 ("The company had received in-principle approval from Sebi for the MF foray on 4 October 2024") and BS 3 Jan 2024 ("filed the application for MF licence on October 19, 2023"). The reg. 7 amendment (26 Jun 2023) came about four months before the filing, and it applied to every applicant. The Angel One comparator is correct: Cafemutual 14 Feb 2023 says it "applied for MF licence in September 2021" and got in-principle approval "vide their letter dated February 8, 2023", and BS/PTI 26 Nov 2024 gives the CoR as 25 Nov 2024. That is about 17 months to in-principle and 21.5 to final. The Zerodha figure (~23 months) is still unopened and should not be used. The date problem is the choice of controls. Bajaj, Angel One, Old Bridge and Zerodha all got in-principle approval before the 2023 SEBI speed-up reported in BS 3 Jan 2024 ("Lately, Sebi has quickened licence approvals"). The one control from Jio's own cohort, Capitalmind, was opened and is left out of the strongestCase. JFS being "under two years old as a listed entity" is true but misleading: it listed in Aug 2023 and applied two months later. The co-sponsor BlackRock and JFS's NBFC predecessor both predate that.
verdicts.identityTest: The entities match. Jio BlackRock Asset Management is the 50:50 JFS–BlackRock JV named in BS 27 May 2025, and the applicant in BS 3 Jan 2024 is "Jio Financial, which has a joint venture (JV) with Blackrock Financial Management". The problem is the phrase "the Ambani connection", which makes a family the actor. The only Ambani in the record is Isha Ambani, as a Non-Executive Director of JFS (mandates-ventures c044). No document places any Ambani in contact with SEBI about this licence. The phrase can survive as a narrative label only. It must never be turned into an edge.
verdicts.baseRate:
The narrative's comparison set is n=2 to 4, all from before the speed-up. The fair set is the 2024 in-principle cohort, which I checked in BS articles.
- Capitalmind, an unconnected Bengaluru PMS firm, was in the same in-principle queue as Jio at 30 Jun 2024. BS 26 Aug 2024: "three other applicants were in the fray for in-principle approval as of June 30. These companies included the Jio Financial and BlackRock Financial joint venture". Capitalmind got in-principle approval on 26 Aug 2024, about 5.5 weeks BEFORE Jio, even though Jio had been queued since Oct 2023. Its final approval came on 14 Apr 2025 (BS 14 Apr 2025), a final leg of about 7.6 months against Jio's 7.7.

In the post-speed-up cohort with known dates, a final leg of about 7.5–8 months occurs in 2 of 2 (Jio, Capitalmind). The property does not discriminate. On the in-principle leg Jio was overtaken by a later, unconnected filer. The narrative's line "faster than every comparator whose dates are known" (and c033's "on the final leg it was faster than every comparator whose dates are known") is false once Capitalmind is counted.

verdicts.innocentReading: From 2023 SEBI shortened MF licence timelines for all applicants (BS 3 Jan 2024; BS 7 Nov 2023: the queue "thinned down due to quick clearances by the Securities and Exchange Board of India"). The final leg is now a six-month inspection after in-principle approval plus processing (BS 7 Jan 2025). Jio BlackRock's 7.7 months matches unconnected Capitalmind's 7.6. A well-capitalised JV whose co-sponsor previously ran an Indian AMC (DSP BlackRock), and which had already hired its CEO and CIO, would be expected to finish at the fast end of that standard window. The investment-adviser and broking registrations are separate routine processes that followed the JV's own schedule.

Neither says anything about Jio BlackRock, so sourceCheck is 'partially'. The strongestCase depends on controls from before the 2023 SEBI speed-up. verdicts.dateTest: Actor: BJP (a party statement, with national spokesperson Sambit Patra quoted). Did: called OCCRP a US 'deep state' media tool to 'destabilise India by targeting Prime Minister Modi'. When: 7 Dec 2024. ThePrint of 7 Dec 2024 reports it: "The Deep State had a clear objective to destabilise India by targeting Prime Minister Modi" and "OCCRP has served as a media tool for carrying out a deep state agenda". The dates line up. Drop Site published on 2 Dec 2024, five days before the BJP statement. The BJP's "50% ... from the U.S. State Department" traces to that reporting. OCCRP's FAQ was updated on 7 Dec 2024, the same day. The Adani stock story (31 Aug 2023) came 15 months before the US indictment (Nov 2024), and the two cover different subjects: FPI stock trading versus solar-contract bribery. The chronology passes, but putting the two side by side in strongestCase implies a link that no source makes.
verdicts.identityTest: OCCRP (Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project) is the same body in all three sources. The BJP is the party as an institution, and Patra is named. The US government funders are named in Drop Site as USAID, State Department and others. There is no mismatch between entities. One problem: the file's source title lists NDR as a co-publisher, but the Drop Site page as fetched names only Mediapart, Il Fatto Quotidiano and Reporters United. Verify NDR or drop it. No family, religion or ethnicity is framed as the actor.
verdicts.baseRate: The property is majority government funding of an investigative non-profit. It is common in donor-funded media development in post-Soviet, Balkan and other low-philanthropy regions, but not near-universal among global investigative consortia. ICIJ, for example, runs on philanthropy. So 52% does set OCCRP apart as a funding dependency. It says nothing about editorial direction. The SPEC's symmetry control applies directly: the "Soros funds a campaign" lens, run on OCCRP's other listed funders (OSF, the Dutch, Swedish, UK and NZ governments, MacArthur), would produce the same "foreign instrument" reading for every funder. Funding alone therefore cannot tell direction from dependency.
verdicts.denialFound: Yes, and it is recorded. OCCRP told ThePrint (7 Dec 2024): "The U.S. government, while providing some funding to OCCRP, has no say in our editorial processes and no control over our reporting." The US State Department spokesperson said: "It's disappointing that the ruling party in India would make these kinds of accusations" (https://theprint.in/diplomacy/attempt-to-destabilise-india-bjp-claims-us-state-dept-targeting-country-with-adani-indictment/2392501/). OCCRP's FAQ (updated 7 Dec 2024) says: "Donors never have access to editorial meetings or any aspect of our editorial process". On key personnel it says "a disagreement with a donor over a grant's 'key personnel' has never taken place". The OCCRP board, quoted in Drop Site, says "no donor has ever vetoed any staff position".
verdicts.innocentReading: OCCRP took US grants, like most of its peer outlets, because regional philanthropy is thin, and it publishes its funders. USAID's key-personnel approval is a standard term in US cooperative agreements, not editorial control. The Adani story was built on bank and fund records shared with the Guardian and the FT. The US indictment came from a separate DOJ/SEC process on a different subject. The BJP statement is ordinary partisan counter-framing after Congress used OCCRP and indictment material against the government.
verdicts.reason: The core record holds. ThePrint confirms the BJP allegation (date, words, the "50%" citation). Drop Site confirms the funding figures word for word: "Between 2014 and 2023, the American federal government provided 52 percent of the money actually spent by OCCRP"; 46.4% on OCCRP's basis; 63% in 2016; "at least $47 million" since 2008; Gaydosik's quote on key personnel; and the board's no-veto statement. The narrative correctly separates dependency, which is evidenced, from direction, which is not, and a 'contested' status with 'alleged' as the underlying tier fits. What stops a clean pass is two defects. (1) The claim says the funding dependency is "documented (52%)", but the file's own edge c016 tiers it 'reported': it rests on a single journalist consortium's analysis of OCCRP's financials, not a primary audited filing. (2) strongestCounter says the US is India's "largest defence and technology partner". SIPRI's March 2025 fact sheet contradicts this: India's main suppliers in 2020–24 were "Russia 36 France 33 Israel 13", so the US is not in the top three. The sentence is also argument rather than evidence. The State Department's quoted words are "disappointing that the ruling party in India would make these kinds of accusations". That is a rebuke, not the explicit denial of editorial influence the file paraphrases.
verdicts.corrections: 1. Change the claim text "funding dependency documented (52%)" to "funding dependency reported (52%, Drop Site consortium analysis, 2 Dec 2024)", in line with c016's tier 'reported'. 2. In strongestCounter, delete "a state that wished to 'destabilise' India would not be simultaneously its largest defence and technology partner". If a symmetry point is wanted, replace it with a sourced fact such as "SIPRI 2020–24: US not among India's top three arms suppliers (Russia 36%, France 33%, Israel 13%), though India is shifting toward Western suppliers" (https://www.sipri.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/fs_2503_at_2024_0.pdf), or drop the argument entirely. 3. In strongestCounter and c017, replace "the US State Department denies editorial influence" with the quoted words "It's disappointing that the ruling party in India would make these kinds of accusations" (ThePrint, 7 Dec 2024). Keep any 'supports professional development' wording only if a source containing it is opened. 4. In strongestCase, qualify the Adani indictment point: it was a DOJ/SEC action on alleged US$265m solar-contract bribery, a different subject from OCCRP's Aug 2023 FPI/stock story, and no source links the two. 5. In the Drop Site source title, check the NDR co-publisher credit; the fetched page names only Mediapart, Il Fatto Quotidiano and Reporters United. 6. Add to baseRate/symmetry that the same funding-equals-direction lens applied to OCCRP's non-US funders (OSF, Sida, Dutch MFA, UK FCDO) yields the same reading, which is why funding share alone cannot settle direction.

verdicts.dateTest: Written as a claim: SEBI (WTM Kamlesh C. Varshney) disposed of two show-cause proceedings "without any direction" on 18 Sep 2025, and the Supreme Court (Vishal Tiwari v UoI) ruled on 3 Jan 2024. The SEBI order says: "WTM/KV/CFID/CFID-SEC1/31672/2025-26 ... DATE: September 18, 2025". The Adicorp order is WTM/KV/CFID/CFID-TPD/31671/2025-26, same date. AEL told the exchanges on 19 Sep 2025. ThePrint dates the expert-committee report 19 May 2023. The Lokpal order is dated 28 May 2025. The dates in the narrative hold. The problem is that the record is stale for its own asOf of 26 Sep 2026. It leaves out three later events. (1) On 22 Sep 2026 five Adani firms (AEL, Adani Green, Adani Total Gas, AWL Agri, Adani Energy Solutions) settled Hindenburg-linked SEBI adjudication proceedings for Rs 1.51 crore under SCN dated 15 Feb 2024. The proceedings covered RPT disclosure (Adani Estates–Vakoder, FY13) and audit reports signed without peer review in 2015–21 (Business Standard 22 Sep 2026; also PTI, The Hindu, Indian Express, ThePrint). (2) On 10 Sep 2026 Karan Adani and B Ravi settled the PMC Projects matter. (3) The FPI strand is not merely "not located". It is live: SEBI rejected settlement applications from 13 offshore funds in Aug 2026 (ET via Business Standard/Bloomberg 24 Aug 2026; Reuters 24 Aug 2026), and five funds took SEBI to SAT in June 2026 and withdrew in Aug 2026. The narrative's "US SEC/DOJ matters" line is also out of date: a US judge dismissed the criminal case against Gautam and Sagar Adani on 10–11 Aug 2026 (Reuters, BBC).
verdicts.identityTest: The noticees match the sources, identified by PAN: APSEZ AAACG7917K, Adani Power AABCA2957L, AEL AABCA2804L, Gautam S. Adani ABKPA0965H, Rajesh S. Adani, Jugeshinder Singh, Milestone Tradelinks AACCM9423C and Rehvar Infrastructure AADCR6843C. The Adicorp order names Adicorp Enterprises Pvt Ltd. The AEL intimation (CIN L51100GJ1993PLC019067) attaches order WTM/KV/CFID/CFID-SEC1/31672/2025-26. The SC judgment is the right one (CJI Chandrachud, 3 Jan 2024). It records "twenty-two out of the twenty-four investigations" as complete, and SEBI said in Nov 2024 that all 24 were complete. One sourcing gap: the Adicorp order is cited in the narrative but not linked in its srcs. It exists at sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/sep-2025/order_matter_adicorp.pdf.
verdicts.baseRate: Not a base-rate claim. For symmetry, the same "not established on a point of law, not exoneration on the facts" reading applies to any LODR RPT case from before the 2021 amendment. The order records Adani's argument that SEBI's past precedents consistently read the pre-2021 definition narrowly. So the prospective-amendment point is general, not Adani-specific. The SC's standard ("does not inspire confidence" in third-party reports as proof that SEBI's probe was inadequate) is a transfer-of-investigation threshold that would bind any petitioner equally. The claim names no family, religion or ethnicity as the actor: "Adani" here means the listed group and its named noticees.
verdicts.denialFound: Adani's reading is on record but missing from the narrative. Gautam Adani, 18 Sep 2025, as reported by NDTV: "Hindenburg claims were baseless", i.e. SEBI "reaffirmed" the group's position (headline seen via Google News; full text not fetched). The Business Standard piece of 24 Aug 2026 says "The conglomerate has denied any links to the funds" and "The ports-to-power conglomerate repeatedly denied those allegations". The same piece says SEBI, Adani and the 13 funds did not respond to ET or Bloomberg on the FPI settlement rejections, so they were asked and did not answer. No statement from the petitioner's side (Prashant Bhushan) on the 2025 orders was located.
verdicts.innocentReading: The "clean chit" framing and the "technicality" framing each hold part of the record. The primary orders do more than decide a point of law. Both orders (Milestone/Rehvar para 59.2(ii); Adicorp para 89.2) say: "On merit too, it is held that impugned transactions cannot be classified as manipulative or fraudulent transactions ... since (i) there is no allegation of siphoning off of money or diversion of fund; (ii) all the money has come back with interest before the start of the investigation". So the claim-text phrase "not a merits finding" is wrong as applied to the SEBI orders. It is accurate only for the SC, which states: "This Court has not interfered with the outcome of the investigations". The boring explanation: a regulator applied the rule in force in 2018–19, found the loans repaid with interest, and found no fraud evidence beyond the classification charge. At the same time it kept other Hindenburg-derived proceedings open, settling some for money (Sep 2026) and refusing to settle others (the FPI strand, Aug 2026). That is neither a blanket exoneration nor a cover-up.
verdicts.reason: The primary source contradicts one element of the claim text. The claim says the 2025 SEBI orders were "true ... on a point of law; not a merits finding". Both 18 Sep 2025 orders contain an explicit PFUTP holding: "On merit too, it is held that impugned transactions cannot be classified as manipulative or fraudulent". That holding is limited, since the orders note the SCN offered no evidence beyond the RPT-classification charge, but it is a merits holding. The narrative also leaves out documented events inside its own asOf (26 Sep 2026). Five Adani firms paid Rs 1.51 crore on 22 Sep 2026 to settle Hindenburg-linked RPT-disclosure and audit proceedings, which directly qualifies "clean chit". And the FPI strand is known to be pending, with settlement applications from 13 funds rejected in Aug 2026, so "not located" understates what is known. The overall "contested" verdict survives and should not be killed. The SC half is confirmed: "does not inspire confidence" (para 40); probe of Hindenburg's short positions (para 67(i)); plea to revoke FPI/LODR amendments "must fail"; "has not interfered with the outcome". The ThePrint and Lokpal sources also confirm what they are cited for. But the claim text as written misstates one primary source and is stale, so it fails.

The primary ground was that pre-2021 LODR did not treat transactions via unrelated parties as RPTs; a secondary 'on merit' PFUTP holding rested on the funds being repaid with interest and on the SCN offering no fraud evidence beyond the RPT charge. (5) Add the Adani response ("Hindenburg claims were baseless", Gautam Adani, 18 Sep 2025, NDTV) as the party's reading. (6) Add a source for "Hindenburg closed Jan 2025" (15 Jan 2025 announcement), or drop it.
