verdicts.dateTest: The claim, restated: BIS CGFS 66 (published 13 May 2021) plus five SEBI shareholding-pattern filings show that BlackRock's presence in Indian equities is structural index weight, not control. The publication date checks out: the BIS landing page reads 'CGFS Papers 66 Date Published 13 May 2021'. The recorded srcs URL (https://www.bis.org/publ/cgfs66.pdf) now returns a 301 redirect to an HTML landing page. The actual 98-page PDF is at https://www.bis.org/publications/cgfs-paper-66-changing-patterns-capital-flows.pdf. The holders filings behind the '0 of 5' figure do not share one snapshot date. Reliance and HDFC Bank are as of 30.06.2026, ITC and Bharti Airtel as of 31.12.2025, and SBI as of 31.03.2025, which is 15 months older than the latest. The 5-company figure mixes three quarters, and the SBI data point is stale. No overlap problem otherwise, because the claim has no tenure.
verdicts.identityTest: cap:blackrock is recorded as 'BlackRock, Inc.' with no identifiers (lei null). SEBI shareholding patterns name holders by fund vehicle and PAN, not by parent manager. So 'BlackRock named ≥1% in 0 of 5' means no single BlackRock or iShares vehicle crosses the per-entity 1% disclosure line. It does not mean BlackRock, Inc.'s combined holding is below 1%. holders.json itself concedes this: its symmetry note says the result reflects 'fragmentation across many separately registered FPI vehicles, none individually crossing 1%'. I re-opened two filings. Reliance SHP 30.06.2026: zero hits for BlackRock or iShares. HDFC Bank SHP 30.06.2026: zero BlackRock hits, and the two Vanguard lines exist ('VANGUARD TOTAL INTERNATIONAL STOCK INDEX FUND … 1.25' and 'VANGUARD EMERGING MARKETS STOCK INDEX FUND … 1.19'). The named-holder facts hold. The step from 'no named vehicle' to 'no proprietary or controlling presence' is an identity-level jump the filings cannot support.
verdicts.baseRate: In the same 5-filing sample, the SPEC controls score as follows: BlackRock named ≥1% in 0 of 5, Vanguard 1 of 5, NBIM 2 of 5, GIC 2 of 5, LIC 4 of 5. Capital Group and Fidelity are required controls in the SPEC but have no base-rate row, so the symmetry check is incomplete. Any manager spread across many FPI vehicles will tend to fall below the per-vehicle 1% line, so 'not named' does not measure how much a manager holds in total. The sample is 5 of 50 NIFTY constituents (10%). The claim's own killIf admits the pattern is untested across the index.
verdicts.denialFound: None found; BlackRock was not asked. No BlackRock statement on its Indian holdings or voting was located or cited. The contrary academic position exists and is not cited: Fichtner, Heemskerk and Garcia-Bernardo, 'Hidden power of the Big Three?' (Business and Politics, 2017), https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/business-and-politics/article/hidden-power-of-the-big-three-passive-index-funds-reconcentration-of-corporate-ownership-and-new-financial-risk/30AD689509AAD62F5B677E916C28C4B6. It argues that passive managers use centralised voting and private engagement as a form of 'hidden power'. That directly contests the claim's 'not control' sentence.
verdicts.innocentReading: The record's own innocent reading fits. Index managers turn up in every large Indian stock at small weights because they replicate MSCI or FTSE India, and those stakes are split across many separately registered vehicles. That is how index investing works, not a buying strategy. The reading cuts both ways, though. Because the stakes are split up, the filings also cannot show how large BlackRock's combined holding or voting weight is. The evidence is consistent with 'small' and equally with 'not observable at this threshold'.
verdicts.reason: The claim credits BIS with a conclusion the paper does not reach. CGFS 66 treats passive flows as a stability risk ('old risks in new clothes'), not as benign. It says nothing about ownership, control or voting, and it never mentions BlackRock or Vanguard. The phrases 'structural, not proprietary' and 'not control' are the analyst's own. The quoted phrase is also not in the paper. The claim quotes 'passive investment strategies … can trigger herd behavior when index rebalancing occurs'. The paper says: 'Passive investment strategies and other practices in the asset management industry can give rise to herd behaviour and contagion, such as when changes to a bond or equity index trigger a rebalancing by the portfolio investors tracking the index.' The India evidence ('0 of 5 named ≥1%') reflects the per-vehicle disclosure threshold and says nothing about BlackRock's combined stake. The 'not control' sentence is contested by named literature that the record does not cite. The underlying comparison is still legitimate as analysis: the holders facts are documented, and the BAT (22.91%) and Pastel/Singtel (7.49%) contrasts check out. So the claim stays at analytic, but only after it is rewritten.
verdicts.corrections: (1) srcs: replace https://www.bis.org/publ/cgfs66.pdf, which redirects to an HTML page, with https://www.bis.org/publications/cgfs-paper-66-changing-patterns-capital-flows.pdf. (2) d: replace the invented quotation with the verbatim sentence: 'Passive investment strategies and other practices in the asset management industry can give rise to herd behaviour and contagion, such as when changes to a bond or equity index trigger a rebalancing by the portfolio investors tracking the index.' Replace 'rather than banks' with the actual wording: 'An increasing share of foreign capital has been channelled through investment funds and other portfolio investors. Indeed, in many countries, portfolio investors have surpassed banks as the largest source of foreign credit.' (3) lab: remove 'the BIS reading'. Suggested wording: 'Analytic: passive-fund presence in five NIFTY 50 filings is fragmented benchmark weight; CGFS 66 supplies the flow mechanism (and flags it as a volatility risk), not a control finding.' (4) d: add that 'named ≥1%' is a per-vehicle SEBI disclosure threshold and that BlackRock's combined stake was not measured. Add the snapshot dates (SBI 31.03.2025; ITC and Bharti 31.12.2025; RIL and HDFC Bank 30.06.2026). (5) Soften the sentence 'An index fund's stake is its clients' money voting a benchmark weight, not control' to 'confers no board seat or promoter status in the filings opened'. Cite Fichtner, Heemskerk and Garcia-Bernardo (2017) as the contrary view on voting and engagement power. (6) upgradeIf and killIf are inverted. BlackRock at ≥5% in many constituents, or a board seat, would refute this claim, so that belongs in killIf. Full-index data confirming the pattern would strengthen the claim, so that belongs in upgradeIf. Also add to killIf: combined BlackRock, Inc. holdings, from its N-PORT or fund holdings, at ≥1–2% of many NIFTY 50 constituents. (7) Symmetry: add Capital Group and Fidelity rows to holders.json baseRates as the SPEC requires. (8) Add a 'contra'/denial note: BlackRock not asked.

verdicts.dateTest: Written out, the claim is: Madhabi Puri Buch (with Dhaval Buch) held units in GDOF, an IPE Plus / Global Opportunities Fund structure, from 2015 to 2018. Her SEBI roles were whole-time member from April 2017 and chairperson from 2 March 2022 to 28 February 2025. SEBI's Adani investigation followed the January 2023 Hindenburg report. The holding and her whole-time member tenure overlap for about one year (2017-2018). The holding does NOT overlap her chairpersonship or the 2023 Adani probe. LiveLaw reports the allegation this way: "invested Rs. 5 crore in 2015 and held till 2018". Buch's response was that it was "redeemed in 2018, two years before SEBI's investigation began". So the claim's core link, a conflict that let the chair go easy on the 2023 Adani probe, depends on a holding that ended about four years before she became chair. The record's strongestCounter ("before any regulatory role existed to create a conflict") also overstates things, because it ignores the 2017-18 overlap.
verdicts.identityTest: The actor is correct. Madhabi Puri Buch was SEBI chairperson from March 2022 to February 2025. Both sources name her and Dhaval Buch. The fund is GDOF, which Hindenburg says Vinod Adani also used, via IPE Plus / Anil Ahuja. The narrative's "associate of Vinod Adani" is a loose but fair paraphrase of Hindenburg. The Cals Refineries FIR (March 2025) is correctly kept apart as a different matter.
verdicts.baseRate: No comparative dataset exists on SEBI or RBI heads' pre-appointment offshore or fund holdings, so this cannot be computed. It is also not a discriminating property. Senior regulators hired from the private sector (Buch came from ICICI and Greater Pacific Capital) routinely bring legacy investments, ESOPs and spousal consulting income. Legacy holdings like these are the norm for private-sector appointees, and that is why disclosure and recusal regimes exist. In the SPEC symmetry control, Tyagi, Buch and Pandey are all public roles, and the same rule applies to each: allegations against any of them are 'alleged' and carry the recorded response. Applied the same way, the lens gives no stronger reading for Buch than an unadjudicated allegation.
verdicts.denialFound: Yes, the Buchs responded directly. NewsOnAir (govt.) reports: "Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) Chairperson Madhabi Puri Buch and her husband Dhaval Buch have denied allegations against them by short-seller Hindenburg Research… The alleged investments reportedly date back to 2015, well before Madhabi Buch's appointment as a full-time member of SEBI in 2017." (https://www.newsonair.gov.in/hindenburg-research-firm-alleges-sebi-chairperson-madhabi-puri-buch-spouse-dhaval-buch-owned-stakes-in-offshore-entities-linked-to-adani-group). Before the Lokpal she said "she was not involved in any SEBI proceedings related to the Adani Group and had no control over the fund's investments, being a mere passive investor". The Lokpal's order of 28 May 2025 then found "no material suggesting quid pro quo or conflict of interest" and called the complaints "unverified and flimsy or fragile allegations" (https://www.livelaw.in/top-stories/lokpal-dismisses-complaints-against-sebi-chariperson-madhabi-puri-buch-hindenburg-research-adani-group-293764).
verdicts.innocentReading: A former private-sector banker made a passive, legacy investment in 2015 in a fund run by her husband's acquaintance. She redeemed it in 2018, shortly after joining SEBI as a whole-time member and years before she became chair or the Adani probe began. SEBI's Adani actions were decided by other whole-time members and panels. The Supreme Court's expert committee (May 2023) and its January 2024 judgment did not find regulatory failure. SEBI's September 2025 orders dismissed the related-party-transaction allegations, and other Hindenburg-linked matters were settled. None of this requires the chair to have gone easy on anyone.
verdicts.reason: The claim says the allegations "show" that the chair had a financial conflict "that let her go easy on the Adani investigation". Neither cited source supports that. NewsOnAir reports only the allegation and the Buchs' denial. LiveLaw reports that the Lokpal, the only body to adjudicate it, found "no material suggesting quid pro quo or conflict of interest". Three things are true separately: the 2015-18 holding, her later chairpersonship, and the Adani probe. The claim joins them into a causal link none of the sources makes, and the dates break that link, since the holding ended about four years before she became chair. As a fact the claim is refuted. It survives only as a narrative, at tier 'alleged' (Hindenburg, a named short-seller, asserts it), with the Lokpal dismissal as the required contra. It is not an edge.
verdicts.corrections: 1) status "contested" is not a CONTRACT tier. Set tier to "alleged" with contra = the Lokpal order of 28 May 2025 (LiveLaw URL). 2) Reword the claim as an attribution: "Hindenburg (10 Aug 2024) alleged that SEBI chair Buch had a conflict of interest over the Adani probe because of a 2015-18 GDOF holding; she denied it and the Lokpal dismissed the complaints (28 May 2025)". Drop "show" and "let her go easy". 3) In strongestCounter, change "before any regulatory role existed to create a conflict" to say the holding ran until 2018 and overlapped roughly one year of her whole-time-member tenure (from April 2017), but not her chairpersonship (from March 2022) or the 2023 Adani probe. 4) In strongestCounter, "unverified presumption" should be the Lokpal's actual words, "unverified and flimsy or fragile allegations". 5) "the underlying Adani short-selling allegations themselves were dismissed by SEBI's final orders in September 2025" is too broad. The 18-19 Sept 2025 orders dismissed the related-party-transaction show-cause notices (Adicorp, Milestone Tradelinks, Rehvar). Other Hindenburg-linked matters were settled (about Rs 1.5 crore, without admission), and the offshore-FPI/MPS strand is separate. Also, the allegations were Hindenburg's, not "short-selling allegations". 6) The SC expert committee (May 2023) said it was "not possible… to conclude that there has been a regulatory failure". That is weaker than "found no regulatory failure", so reword to match. 7) The strongestCase says "SEBI did not publish a recusal record". Add that Buch told the Lokpal she was not involved in Adani proceedings, and that she disclosed and recused on Mahindra matters, which the Lokpal accepted. 8) Add the SEBI Sept 2025 order PDF (https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/sep-2025/order_matter_milestone_rehvar.pdf) to srcs if the counter keeps relying on it.

verdicts.dateTest:
Actor, action and date: SEBI (board and circulars) eased the Aug 2023 FPI granular-disclosure framework, 2024-25. SEBI is the correct actor throughout. The easing steps are:
(1) A consultation paper on 27 Feb 2024, followed by a board decision and circular in Mar 2024 (board meeting 15 Mar 2024). This created the no-identified-promoter exemption, with a 3% composite cap on the apex company.
(2) A university-fund exemption by circular on 1 Aug 2024 (EY: "Circular issued by the SEBI on 1 August 2024 granting exemption to University Funds").
(3) A consultation paper on 30 Jul 2024 about size-criterion FPIs, then another on 10 Jan 2025 proposing Rs 25k to 50k cr, then board approval on 24 Mar 2025 (BusinessToday, 24 Mar 2025), then a circular around 9 Apr 2025.
The chronology holds. One detail is wrong: the narrative says the change came "within about 19 months of the original circular taking effect". It was 19 months after the circular was issued (24 Aug 2023) but about 17 months after it took effect (the SOP was adopted 27 Oct 2023 and the rules applied from Nov 2023). Separately, c020 cites the 30 Jul 2024 consultation paper as the lead-in to the threshold doubling. The direct lead-in was the 10 Jan 2025 paper. The July 2024 paper proposed a different fix: disclose only enough to establish land-border-country (LBC) status.
verdicts.identityTest:
The entity is right: SEBI, under chairs Madhabi Puri Buch (the 2024 steps) and Tuhin Kanta Pandey (the Mar 2025 doubling). The rule is right too: SEBI circular of 24 Aug 2023 on additional disclosures by FPIs.
There is an identity problem inside the narrative, though. It treats the size criterion as "the post-Hindenburg transparency reform". SEBI's own 30 Jul 2024 consultation paper says the size-based disclosures "were prescribed with a view to identify and categorise these FPIs as LBC or Non-LBC entities". That is the Press Note 3 (China) purpose. The Adani/MPS-relevant piece is the 50% concentration criterion, and it was kept (Business Upturn: "SEBI clarified in its press release that no changes are being made to the 50% group-level concentration threshold"). So the rule that was loosened is mostly not the Hindenburg-driven one.
verdicts.baseRate:
Reviewing a threshold after implementation is routine at SEBI. SEBI runs "ease of doing business" consultation papers on nearly every new disclosure framework within 1-2 years of launch, and fixed rupee thresholds get revised as markets grow. Cash-market volume rose 122% (Pandey, BusinessToday) and average daily turnover was Rs 1.18 trillion in Dec 2024. Easing after consulting the industry is well over 80% of how SEBI frameworks develop, so it does not by itself show capture.
The SPEC control ("record who asked") comes out the same way. SEBI's Feb 2024 paper says: "During interactions with industry participants, the case for enhancing ease of doing business in respect of Category I University Funds ... and in respect of FPIs with concentrated holdings in listed entities without an identified promoter was made." Its Jul 2024 paper says: "during interactions with industry participants, challenges have been identified ... very large non-exempt funds have breached the size criteria". The Jan 2025 paper drew comments from 31 respondents (DDPs, custodians, industry associations, FPIs), with feedback reported as broadly positive. Industry asked, and SEBI records that it did. No individual lobbyist is named.
verdicts.denialFound: SEBI's stated rationale, not a denial of the narrative. BusinessToday (24 Mar 2025) quotes Pandey: "The average trading volume in the cash market has increased by 122 per cent". SEBI's press release, as reported by Business Upturn (https://businessupturn.com/finance/stock-market/sebi-retains-rule-mandating-additional-disclosures-by-fpis-holding-over-50-equity-aum-in-a-single-corporate-group/), says "no changes are being made to the 50% group-level concentration threshold". I found no record of SEBI being asked directly whether the changes undo the post-Hindenburg reform, so none was found and it was not asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: The Aug 2023 framework was built quickly and had two separate tests. The concentration test addresses MPS/SAST evasion by promoters, the Adani concern. The size test addresses LBC/Press Note 3 screening. Once it was running, very large, widely held funds (for example university endowments, and funds concentrated in companies with no promoter) were caught even though they carry none of the promoter round-tripping risk. SEBI consulted in public three times (Feb 2024, Jul 2024, Jan 2025) and exempted only those classes, each with conditions (India AUM under 25% of global AUM; a 3% cap on the apex company). It also indexed the size threshold to market growth. The concentration test that caught Adani-linked FPIs was left as it was. The same board meeting set up a conflict-of-interest committee for SEBI's own leadership.
verdicts.reason:
The claim as worded fails on two of its three parts.
- "Quietly" is false. Every step went through a published consultation paper, a board press release and a circular.
- "Undoing the post-Hindenburg transparency reform" is contradicted by the primary record. The 50% concentration criterion, the part aimed at promoter round-tripping, was kept. The size criterion that was doubled exists for LBC/Press Note 3 screening, per SEBI's own Jul 2024 paper.
- "Under industry pressure" is partly supported, and the file currently understates it. SEBI's own Feb 2024 and Jul 2024 papers say industry participants made the case for the university-fund and no-promoter exemptions and raised the size-criterion burden. "Pressure", as opposed to ordinary consultation, is characterisation with no named lobby submission behind it.
What survives is a documented fact pattern: a real, industry-requested easing of parts of the framework. The inference that this undid the Hindenburg-era reform is not supported. That leaves an analytic reading at most, and the narrative's status of "contested" is defensible only if the sentence is scored as partly true with a false framing.
Sources checked: the BusinessToday piece opened via WebFetch (curl got a 403) and confirms the threshold change and the 122% figure. Business Upturn confirms the concentration test was kept. Neither says "industry pressure" or "undoing".
verdicts.corrections:
1. strongestCase: change "within about 19 months of the original circular taking effect" to "about 19 months after the Aug 2023 circular was issued (about 17 months after it took effect)". Add that SEBI's own 27 Feb 2024 consultation paper (§3.2, https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/feb-2024/1709046675449.pdf) and 30 Jul 2024 paper (§3.1-3.2, https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/jul-2024/1722335744572.pdf) record that "industry participants" made the case for these exemptions. That is the documented "who asked", and it is stronger than the current text.
2. whatWouldChangeThis: delete the premise that no industry ask is on record. Reframe it as needing a named FPI or industry-body submission.
3. c020: change the "Who asked" line. The direct lead-in to the Rs 50k cr change was SEBI's consultation paper of 10 Jan 2025 (comments due 31 Jan 2025; 31 commenters). The 30 Jul 2024 paper proposed a narrower LBC-only disclosure. Also replace "no specific FPI or industry body's submission is named" with "SEBI's Feb and Jul 2024 papers state that industry participants raised these issues; no individual submitter is named".
4. strongestCounter: add that the size criterion was intended for LBC/Press Note 3 categorisation, not MPS/promoter round-tripping (Jul 2024 paper §2.2), so doubling it does not touch the Hindenburg-relevant test.
5. Add sources to the narrative's srcs: the two SEBI consultation-paper PDFs above, and the SEBI circular of Mar 2024 (https://www.sebi.gov.in/legal/circulars/mar-2024/amendment-to-circular-for-mandating-additional-disclosures-by-fpis-that-fulfil-certain-objective-criteria_82418.html). Add indiacorplaw (11 May 2025) as critical commentary that the threshold rise weakens Press Note 3 safeguards.
6. Status: keep it "contested" only with an explicit note that "quietly" and "undoing" are contradicted by the primary record, while "industry-requested easing" is documented. Any edge derived from this should be tier analytic with the innocentReading above, never alleged or reported wrongdoing.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated: "Government of India [with Mauritius, then Singapore] designed the 2016 treaty protocols [signed 10 May 2016 for Mauritius, 30 Dec 2016 for Singapore] so that round-tripped money already in India would escape source taxation." The dates are correct. The Mauritius protocol was signed on 10 May 2016, the cutoff is shares acquired on or after 1 April 2017, and the Singapore treaty's capital-gains article is linked to the Mauritius one. The date test passes, but it is the only part of the claim that does.
verdicts.identityTest: The claim names no specific actor. "Designed to" puts intent on the negotiating governments (the Finance Ministry/CBDT) without naming anyone or any submission, and the claim names no beneficiary who was round-tripping. So there is nobody to check against a CIN, DIN or office-with-dates. The claim fails for lack of an identifiable designer or beneficiary.
verdicts.baseRate: Nearly every treaty or tax-law transition protects existing positions and applies the new rule prospectively. This protocol's own interest clause does the same thing (debt-claims existing before 31 March 2017 stay exempt). The 2018 Budget's long-term capital gains tax on listed equity also protected gains up to 31 Jan 2018 for all investors, domestic ones included. Well over 80% of comparable transitions do this, so grandfathering tells you nothing about intent. The same lens applied to the control would "prove" that every grandfathering clause is designed to favour whoever held assets beforehand, which is absurd.
verdicts.denialFound: No specific denial found. The allegation has not been put to the Government of India, so none was sought. The official stated purpose runs directly against the claim. The Government of India press release of 10 May 2016, as summarised by TaxGuru (https://taxguru.in/income-tax/indiamauritius-dtaa-amended-tackle-tripping-funds.html) and STEP (https://www.step.org/industry-news/mauritius-and-india-agree-taxation-round-tripped-investments), says the protocol aims at "tackling the dual problem of treaty shopping and round tripping of funds." That is a statement of purpose, not a denial.
verdicts.innocentReading: Grandfathering is standard legal-certainty practice. It avoids retroactively taxing gains that thousands of legitimate PE, VC and FPI funds priced under the old treaty, which matters especially after the Vodafone retrospective-tax backlash. The protocol also treated every investor using the route the same way. The grandfathering covers only capital-gains taxing rights on shares. It never protected round-tripped money from source-of-funds liability: the Black Money Act, Income Tax Act s.68/69 on unexplained credits, PMLA and FEMA all still apply. So even as a mechanism, "escape" overstates what the clause did. The honest version is about effect, not design: pre-2017 Mauritius-routed positions, including any round-tripped ones, keep the old capital-gains treatment. GAAR Rule 10U(1)(d) also exempts gains on investments made before 1 April 2017, which widens that effect and should be recorded.
verdicts.reason: The only source (K&L Gates, 18 May 2016) backs the mechanism and nothing more: "Gain from the sale or transfer of shares acquired before April 1, 2017, regardless of when sold or transferred, is 'grandfathered' under the old rules." It says nothing about design intent, round-tripping beneficiaries, or anyone lobbying for the clause. "Designed to let round-tripped money escape" joins a true mechanism to an assumed motive. The record's own strongestCounter and whatWouldChangeThis admit there is no evidence of intent. The official stated purpose was the opposite: to tackle round-tripping. Grandfathering is the norm, so it cannot discriminate. "Speculative" is not a contract tier, and the claim as worded has no tier it can hold. Keep only a restated, effect-only analytic narrative.
verdicts.corrections: 1. Change status "speculative" to tier "analytic", or kill it if the "designed to" wording is kept. 2. Rewrite the claim as: "The 2016 India-Mauritius protocol (signed 10 May 2016) and the linked India-Singapore protocol (30 Dec 2016) grandfathered capital gains on shares acquired before 1 April 2017. Any pre-2017 round-tripped holdings therefore kept treaty capital-gains protection. There is no evidence the clause was designed for that purpose." 3. Add innocentReading as above, including that the Black Money Act, s.68/69, PMLA and FEMA are unaffected, and that the interest clause and the 2018 long-term capital gains tax were grandfathered the same way. 4. Add the official purpose statement as contra (Government of India press release of 10 May 2016: "tackling the dual problem of treaty shopping and round tripping of funds"), with TaxGuru or STEP as the secondary source, plus the primary PIB URL once it is retrieved. 5. Note that GAAR Rule 10U(1)(d) also grandfathers pre-1 April 2017 investments. This is a fact that strengthens the effect reading and is currently missing. 6. Add a primary source for the Singapore protocol (CBDT notification or PIB, 30 Dec 2016). At present the only Singapore support is K&L Gates' remark that the Singapore treaty is linked. 7. killIf: the claim as worded (intent) stays unsupported with no documentary evidence of beneficiary submissions shaping the grandfathering clause.

verdicts.dateTest: Written out, the claim is: SEBI, in its January 2018 board decision ("Easing of Access Norms for FPIs"), removed the 20-investor broad-based floor, and this structurally benefited concentrated FPIs holding Adani shares, 2018-2023. The premise is false as stated. The board paper at https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/meetingfiles/jan-2018/1515989011412_1.pdf keeps the definition: a broad-based fund "has at least twenty investors, with no investor holding more than 49%". Para 3.2.4 only extends the existing "deemed to be broad based" treatment. Until then it applied only to funds with a bank investor. The paper widens it to "Sovereign Wealth Fund, Insurance/ Reinsurance Companies, Pension Funds, Exchange Traded Funds". Para 3.2.14 adds a 3-month cure period for a fund that "due to exit of some offshore global investors loses its broad based status". The broad-based condition for Category II was dropped only by the SEBI (FPI) Regulations 2019 (September 2019). The proposals were sent to DEA, DoR and RBI on 24 May 2017, well before the January 2023 Hindenburg report.
verdicts.identityTest: Fails. The claim names the wrong rule. The "2018 amendment" that the SC expert committee, the petitioners and the Supreme Court discussed was the beneficial-owner / "opaque structures" amendment, not the broad-based investor floor. SC judgment of 3 January 2024 (Vishal Tiwari v UoI, para 20, hosted at https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/jan-2024/1704888578340.pdf): "These requirements were amended by SEBI in 2018 and 2019 by removing the requirement of disclosing ownership of the FPIs by a natural person." Para 26: "The 2018 amendment required mandatory disclosures by all FPIs ... It marked a shift towards tightening ... provisions on 'opaque structures' being omitted in 2019." The broad-based rule is not mentioned anywhere in the judgment. The node cap:sebi-fpi-2018-broadbased-amendment mixes up two different rule changes.
verdicts.baseRate: Non-discriminating. The deemed-broad-based extension and the 3-month cure period apply to every Category II fund that has sovereign-wealth, pension, insurer or ETF investors, and that is most of the institutional FPI universe (by count and by AUM, easily over 80%). The change was industry-wide market-access relief, sent to DEA, DoR and RBI in May 2017, with no issuer-specific element. Symmetry: the same lens would tie the 2018 easing to every group with concentrated FPI holders, so it picks out nothing specific to Adani.
verdicts.denialFound: SEBI's position, recorded in the SC judgment of 3 January 2024 (paras 25-27, at https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/jan-2024/1704888578340.pdf): the 2018 amendment "marked a shift towards tightening", and SEBI "claims no disability in its investigation into the Adani group on account of the amendments to the FPI Regulations". SEBI also said the expert committee mistook its use of the word "opaque". The Court held that "The FPI Regulations and LODR Regulations have been tightened by the amendments in question" and refused to order them revoked. The Adani Group rejected the Hindenburg allegations in its 413-page reply, as noted in the LiveLaw source. No party was asked about the broad-based framing specifically; none found, not asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: The January 2018 changes were routine market-access relief. Investor counts in open-ended funds rise and fall, and institutional investors such as SWFs, pension funds and insurers are already regulated. So SEBI treated them like banks when deciding whether a fund is broad-based, and gave funds a cure period instead of automatic reclassification. It was proposed in 2017, long before any Adani allegation. The broad-based label is a registration category, not a beneficial-ownership rule: UBO disclosure under PMLA Rule 9 applied either way.
verdicts.reason: This is decisive on two counts. (1) The Jan 2018 SEBI board paper did not remove the 20-investor floor; it kept that definition and only extended deemed-broad-based status plus added a cure period. (2) The only cited source, LiveLaw of 19 May 2023, never mentions broad-based funds, the 20-investor rule or any 2018 amendment. The primary court record shows that the 2018 amendment at issue was the UBO/opaque-structure change, which SEBI and the Supreme Court call a tightening. Neither the expert committee nor Hindenburg is shown pointing to the broad-based floor. The benefit to grp:adani therefore rests on a mistaken rule and on sources that do not say what the claim says. An "analytic" tier cannot cover a false factual premise.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim as written: "ICEA/IESA lobbied → DPIIT eased PN3 via Press Note 2, March 2026". The only source is a BDO India page reposting The Telegraph, published 12 March 2026. It dates the Cabinet approval to "Tuesday", which is 10 March 2026. The ICEA and IESA quotes are reactions given after that decision, not lobbying before it. The page also says pending applications "will go through the automatic route once the notification is issued", so as of 12 March no notification had been issued. Nothing in the file sources the record's 15 March 2026 notification date or the name "Press Note 2 (2026)". The source gives neither the press-note number nor a notification date. The DPIIT press-notes page loaded but returned no readable 2026 listing (it appears to render with JavaScript). So the event is dated to March 2026 by Cabinet approval, but the number and the 15 March date are unverified. The ordering "after lobbying support" is not shown: the source's timeline has the endorsement coming after the decision.
verdicts.identityTest: The two industry bodies are named correctly. Pankaj Mohindroo is described as "chairman of the India Cellular and Electronics Association", but the record calls him "president", which is wrong. Ashok Chandak as "president of the India Electronics and Semiconductor Association" is correct. The claim tags IESA/ICEA as "electronics/solar PLI manufacturers dependent on Chinese suppliers". The source does not say this. Neither body is a solar association: IESA covers semiconductors and electronics, and ICEA covers mobile phones and electronics. The source mentions ECMS, not PLI, and never mentions dependence on Chinese suppliers. The target node "cap:land-border-investors" is also wrong in substance. According to the source, the relaxation does not cover direct investment by land-border-country investors. DPIIT JS Jai Prakash Shivahare: "All the restrictions for investors from LBCs are still applicable. This relaxation is only for entities in non-LBCs and having beneficial owners from LBCs below 10 per cent and non-controlling stake."
verdicts.baseRate: Industry bodies publicly welcoming a reform that affects their sector is close to universal. Nearly every FDI easing draws favourable quotes from the relevant associations (CII, FICCI, NASSCOM, ICEA and others), so this is non-discriminating (above 80%). A welcome quote after the fact tells us nothing about who asked for the change. The source's own stated driver is structural: about 600 applications had piled up under PN3.
verdicts.denialFound: none found, not asked. There is nothing to deny because the source makes no lobbying allegation. Government's stated rationale, in the BDO/Telegraph piece: the backlog of about 600 pending applications, ease of doing business and manufacturing investment. DPIIT Secretary Amardeep Singh Bhatia and JS Shivahare are quoted (https://www.bdo.in/en-gb/news/2026/india-eases-fdi-rules-under-press-note-3-with-10-per-cent-cap-for-border-country-investors).
verdicts.innocentReading: From 2020 the blanket approval requirement in PN3 also caught global funds and non-LBC entities with small Chinese or Hong Kong LPs or shareholders, and about 600 applications piled up. The government created a 10% non-controlling beneficial-ownership threshold for those non-LBC entities, plus a 60-day track for named manufacturing sectors. Electronics associations welcomed it afterwards, as associations routinely do. Chandak's quote is specifically about "global fund participation", which fits the indirect-beneficial-ownership fix, not Chinese strategic capital.
verdicts.reason: The claim's causal part ("after lobbying support from ICEA and IESA") is not in the only cited source. The source shows the two bodies welcoming the change after the Cabinet decision, which is a reaction, not a request. The claim also misstates the rule. It does not let "land-border-country (incl. China) investors" take automatic-route stakes of up to 10%. It lets non-LBC entities whose LBC beneficial owners hold under 10%, non-controlling, use the automatic route, and DPIIT says all restrictions on LBC investors themselves remain. The "solar", "PLI" and "dependent on Chinese suppliers" descriptors are the author's own additions. The record's tier is "documented", but it rests on a single secondary source: a consulting firm reposting a Telegraph article, with a BDO partner quoted, which gives BDO a self-interest. That is at most "reported" until the DPIIT press note or a PIB release is attached.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Remove "after lobbying support from ICEA and IESA". Replace it with "welcomed after Cabinet approval by ICEA chairman Pankaj Mohindroo and IESA president Ashok Chandak". Change "president" to "chairman" for Mohindroo in entity cap:press-note-2026-easing d[1] and in the claim's d[0]. 2) Rewrite the rule: "non-LBC investing entities with LBC beneficial ownership below 10% and non-controlling may use the automatic route; direct LBC investment still requires government approval; 60-day expedited approval for capital goods, electronic capital goods, electronic components, polysilicon, ingot-wafer." 3) Remove "solar", "PLI" and "dependent on Chinese suppliers". The source mentions none of them (it cites ECMS, raised to ₹40,000 crore), and neither body is a solar association. 4) Change the tier from "documented" to "reported" (one secondary outlet, The Telegraph via BDO, 12 March 2026). To upgrade to documented, attach the DPIIT press note PDF or the PIB Cabinet release. 5) Change "from" from 2026-03-15 to 2026-03-10 (Cabinet approval), unless the notification date is sourced. The "Press Note 2 (2026)" number and the 15 March date are currently unsourced, so either source them or mark them unverified. 6) Reconsider the target node. Better targets are "non-LBC entities with minority LBC beneficial owners" and "global funds with LBC LPs"; cap:land-border-investors as currently written fits poorly. 7) Add the stated driver, "~600 pending applications backlog", as the who-asked or why field required by the SPEC's rule-change control, and add a symmetry note that PN3 (2020) and this easing both came under the same NDA government.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated as: IFSCA issued fund-management regulations for GIFT-IFSC in 2022, and IFSC units get a tax holiday and GST/STT exemptions, which benefits asset managers that move fund vehicles there, from 2022 onward. The start date of 2022 holds. The source says: "Since the introduction of specific regulations for managing funds in 2022, there has been promising investment growth year-on-year." The open end ("to": null) is wrong. The IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2025 repealed and replaced the 2022 Regulations; IFSCA announced the notification in a press release dated 19 Feb 2025. As written, the edge says a repealed instrument is still in force. The tax holiday is also older than the 2022 Regulations. The Section 80LA IFSC deduction predates 2022, so "associated" joins two instruments with separate histories.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity is a statute, so no CIN, DIN or LEI applies. The source never names "IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2022". It says only "specific regulations for managing funds in 2022". The identification is right, but it comes from outside the cited source. The target "cap:fpi-industry" is only a loose fit. The source is about foreign portfolio investors choosing GIFT-IFSC over Mauritius or Singapore. It does not mention "Indian asset managers" or "redomicile". The entity node's FME category details (a USD 75,000 net-worth floor for non-retail, USD 500,000 for retail, USD 5m for Authorised FME for "large managers") are not in the source. They also look garbled: in the 2022 Regulations, the Authorised FME was the category for venture capital and restricted schemes, not "large managers", and the net-worth floors are attached to the wrong categories. The "pass-through tax treatment" line in the entity node is not in the source either.
verdicts.baseRate: This property does not single anyone out. Nearly all international financial centres offer profit-linked tax holidays and exemptions on transaction taxes to attract fund managers: DIFC and ADGM (0% tax regimes), Singapore (13O/13U fund incentives), Luxembourg, Ireland and Mauritius. Over 80% of comparable IFCs share it. Within India, every IFSC unit gets the tax holiday, not only fund managers, so the benefit is not specific to any actor. On the SPEC's rule-change control (record who asked for each easing), the source attributes the push to government policy: "Legal experts and industry players say that the Indian government is pushing GIFT City". It names no lobby. The same reading would apply to any SEZ incentive.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and none is needed: the claim alleges no wrongdoing. The government and IFSCA openly state the aim, which is to bring back onshore the fund activity that was routed through Mauritius, Singapore, Luxembourg and similar centres. The source puts it in these words: "the Indian government is pushing GIFT City over common investment channels through Mauritius, Singapore, the Netherlands, or Luxembourg by offering tax breaks". Nobody has been asked to respond, and no response is required.
verdicts.innocentReading: This is ordinary industrial policy for a financial centre. India offers tax parity or better so that fund structuring, management fees and jobs, which previously went offshore to Mauritius or Singapore, are booked on Indian soil under an Indian regulator. The March 2024 Principal Purpose Test (PPT) amendment to the Mauritius tax treaty, which the source also describes, points the same way: the government tightened the offshore route and eased the onshore one. The fact that asset managers benefit is the stated purpose of the policy, not a hidden transfer to them.
verdicts.reason: The factual core survives. The source confirms that fund-management regulations were introduced in 2022, and it confirms "a 100 percent tax exemption for 10 of the 15-year block period" and "no goods and services tax (GST) or Securities Transaction Tax (STT) on transactions made on IFSC exchanges". One credible outlet makes the claim "reported" as currently sourced; it could move up to "documented" by citing IFSCA's gazette text and Section 80LA. The claim is not refuted, but the record around it overstates its support. (1) It omits that the 2022 Regulations were repealed and replaced in February 2025. (2) The "who benefits" gloss is not in the source: that retail Indian savers reach these funds "only indirectly, if at all", and the word "redomicile". It is also doubtful: Registered FME (Retail) schemes exist, and resident Indians can invest in IFSC funds under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS). That gloss is our own inference and belongs in the analytic tier. (3) The entity node's FME thresholds and the pass-through line are unsourced and appear inaccurate.
verdicts.corrections: 1. On the edge, set "to" to "2025-02" (the 2022 Regulations were repealed by the IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2025, notified in Feb 2025). Either add a successor edge for the 2025 Regulations or relabel the edge to cover the whole FM regime. 2. Split the "d" text: keep the regulations and the tax holiday/GST-STT facts at "reported". Move "who benefits ... not at Indian retail investors" to an analytic note with an innocentReading. Delete "retail Indian savers only reach these funds indirectly, if at all", or source it (it conflicts with the existence of retail FMEs and with LRS access). 3. Replace "redomicile fund vehicles" with the source's framing ("FPIs opting for GIFT IFSC over Mauritius/Singapore routes"), or cite the inbound relocation tax-neutrality provisions directly. 4. State that the tax holiday (Section 80LA) and the GST/STT exemptions apply to all IFSC units and IFSC-exchange transactions, not only fund managers, and that they are separate from the 2022 FM Regulations. 5. On the entity node, delete or re-source the FME net-worth/category bullet (it has no source and the figures look garbled) and the "pass-through tax treatment" claim. Add the IFSCA FM Regulations gazette PDF and the 19 Feb 2025 IFSCA press release (https://www.ifsca.gov.in/Document/Legal/press-release-notification-of-ifsca-fund-management-regulations-202519022025091920.pdf) as primary sources. 6. Upgrade to "documented" only once those primary sources are attached.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: SEBI (board, 209th meeting, chaired by Tuhin Kanta Pandey, who took charge 1 March 2025) raised the FPI size-based granular-disclosure threshold on 24 March 2025. Tenure overlaps. BusinessToday is dated 24 March 2025 and says the change was "announced" that day, without separately dating the board meeting. Business Upturn says "its 209th board meeting held in Mumbai" (published 24 March 2025, updated 14 July 2026). The date passes, but it rests on the press, not the SEBI press release, which I could not reach (the SEBI listing and a guessed URL returned nothing or 404).
verdicts.identityTest: The actor is SEBI (the board), and the subject is FPIs with Indian equity AUM above the threshold. Both sources name the same body and the same instrument (the Aug 2023 additional-disclosure framework for FPIs). There is no identity mismatch. The "Adani-linked FPIs" in the claim are not named or identified in either source.
verdicts.baseRate: This is a rule of general application covering every FPI above the size threshold, so it does not single out any holder or group. Its rationale is scale-driven: BT says "The average trading volume in the cash market has increased by 122 per cent." It supports no inference about who benefited apart from large diversified FPIs in general. Symmetry check under the SPEC's rule-change control: the tightening (Aug 2023, after Hindenburg) and the easing (Mar 2025) both happened under the same NDA-era regulator. No record in the file names who asked for the change. The file already logs that as a gap.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable in the usual sense, since this is a regulatory decision, not an allegation. SEBI's own stated reason is the response on record: the size criterion is being indexed to market growth (cash volumes up 122%), and "no changes are being made to the 50% group-level concentration threshold" (Business Upturn). No one was asked about the "caught the Adani-linked FPIs" framing, and neither source makes that link.
verdicts.innocentReading: A fixed rupee threshold set in 2023 was catching more diversified FPIs each year simply because the market grew. SEBI indexed it upward and explicitly kept the group-concentration test aimed at promoter-linked structuring ("prevent any structuring that could potentially bypass key regulatory guardrails—especially in cases where FPIs are used as vehicles for concentrated promoter interests"). This reads as routine recalibration, not a loosening aimed at any group.
verdicts.reason: The core facts are confirmed by two outlets. BusinessToday: "raise the threshold limit for foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) from the present Rs 25,000 crore of equity AUM" to "FPIs holding more than Rs 50,000 crore of equity AUM ... will now be required to make additional disclosures". Business Upturn: "double the threshold for size-based FPI disclosures from ₹25,000 crore to ₹50,000 crore" and "no changes are being made to the 50% group-level concentration threshold". The claim survives on that. What neither source says is the clause "that caught the Adani-linked FPIs". Neither article mentions Adani; in BT, Adani appears only in unrelated ads on the page. Whether the 50% test actually "caught" Adani-linked FPIs, rather than being designed with them in mind (some funds may have rebalanced to avoid it), is a separate factual claim that needs its own source. "Reducing the number of FPIs required to disclose" is a fair logical consequence, but neither source gives a count. Business Upturn is a thin outlet, and the SEBI board press release, the primary record, is not cited. So the tier holds at reported, not documented. The file record currently says "documented".
verdicts.corrections: 1. The file record's tier ("documented") conflicts with the claim's tier ("reported"). Set it to reported until the SEBI 24 Mar 2025 board-meeting press release (209th meeting) is added as a source. Documented is justified only with that primary source. 2. Reword the Adani clause, both in the text and in d[0] ("the one that actually caught the Adani-linked FPIs"). Use "retaining the 50%-single-corporate-group concentration test introduced in Aug 2023 after the Hindenburg–Adani episode", and cite the SEBI circular of 24 Aug 2023. Alternatively, add a source showing named Adani-linked FPIs were in fact made to disclose under that test; without one, drop "caught". 3. Qualify "reducing the number of FPIs required to disclose" as an inference, or cite a count. 4. Add "209th board meeting" to the record's d field for identity. 5. Keep the "who asked" gap as recorded.

verdicts.identityTest: The actor is SEBI and the instrument is circular SEBI/HO/AFD/AFD-POD-2/P/CIR/2024/104 (EY footnote 2). The governed class is university funds and university-related endowments that are registered, or eligible to register, as Category I FPIs. verdicts.baseRate: Mostly not applicable. This is a regulatory-fact edge, not an inference from a shared property. The August 2023 framework already carved out several classes of FPI (government and government-related entities, and certain listed or regulated pooled vehicles). Adding one more named, conditional class is routine regulatory calibration. On its own it does not point to targeted favouritism. The 25%-of-global-AUM cap keeps out any fund whose book is concentrated in India.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable: there is no accusation to deny. SEBI's stated rationale, via EY, is "enhancing the ease of doing business in India for FPIs", and the exemption was "based on feedback received" on the 27 Feb 2024 consultation paper. None found; SEBI not asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: The boring reading fits. University endowments are large, diversified, tax-exempt non-profits that are hard-pressed to look through to natural persons. SEBI consulted publicly in Feb 2024 and exempted them in Aug 2024 under hard conditions (India equity AUM under 25% of global AUM, global AUM over INR 100 bn, proof of tax-exempt non-profit status, domicile in an eligible jurisdiction). The concentration test that caught the Adani-linked FPIs stays in force for everyone else.
verdicts.reason: The only cited source (EY Regulatory Alert, 06 Aug 2024, PDF at ey.com/content/dam/.../additional-disclosure-framework-for-foreign-portfolio-investors-sebi-consultation-paper.pdf) states the claim nearly word for word. It gives the date, actor, circular number, the exempted class, "subject to compliance with certain conditions", and the three conditions listed on the node. The claim text is a neutral statement of a regulatory fact. It passes. The tier is right at `reported`: one credible professional-services outlet citing the named circular. I could not reach the SEBI primary; two guessed sebi.gov.in URLs returned 404 and the circular listing page returned nothing on universities. The claim can move to `documented` once the SEBI circular itself (SEBI/HO/AFD/AFD-POD-2/P/CIR/2024/104) is cited.
verdicts.corrections: 1) edge d: "US and other university endowments" goes beyond the source. EY says only that funds must be "domiciled in eligible jurisdictions which shall be as specified by SEBI from time to time, in consultation with the CDSSF". Drop "US" or mark it as our inference. 2) edge d: "on the reasoning that non-profit, tax-exempt university funds present a low round-tripping/round-about-promoter risk" is not SEBI's stated reason. The source gives "enhancing the ease of doing business in India for FPIs" and "feedback received" on the 27 Feb 2024 consultation paper. Cyril Amarchand's blog dates that circular to 15 Mar 2024, so from=2024-03-15 holds. The problem is the only cited source. The MoneyLife article is dated 14 January 2025, ten months after the rule, and it covers a different proposal: raising the size threshold from Rs25,000 crore to Rs50,000 crore. verdicts.identityTest: The entity is a SEBI circular and the governed class is registered FPIs, so there is no CIN or DIN to check. The source names a different instrument. MoneyLife covers the January 2025 consultation on the size criterion, and on concentration it says only: "SEBI also clarified that no change is being proposed in the extant threshold or treatment for the concentration criteria, which is designed to prevent circumvention of minimum public shareholding (MPS)..." The article never mentions the March 2024 exemption, "no identified promoter", the apex company, the 3% composite cap, or Adani. The edge is attached to a source about a different rule change.
verdicts.baseRate: Very few Indian listed companies have no identified promoter; widely-held names such as ITC, L&T, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank and Axis Bank are examples. Most listed companies and nearly every family or business group have one: Reliance, Tata, Adani, Birla, Bajaj, Mahindra, Vedanta. So "cannot apply to Adani" is true but does not single Adani out. At least 80% of listed groups are excluded in the same way. The exclusion tells you nothing specific about Adani and cannot serve as Adani-specific evidence in either direction.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. The claim accuses no one. No Adani or SEBI statement tying this exemption to Adani was found, and none was needed or sought.
verdicts.innocentReading: SEBI's stated reason is technical. If a listed company has no promoter, all of its shares count as "public", so FPI concentration in it cannot be used to get around minimum public shareholding (MPS). The 3% composite cap covers the takeover-code (SAST) risk. It is routine ease-of-doing-business relief following the 28 Feb 2024 consultation paper. Nothing indicates it was drafted with Adani in mind, for or against.
verdicts.reason: This fails on the source chain. The only cited source, MoneyLife 76094 (14 Jan 2025), is about the Rs50,000 crore size threshold and says nothing about the March 2024 no-identified-promoter exemption, its conditions, or Adani. The rule itself is real and has a primary record (SEBI circular, March 2024), but the record as filed is not supported by its source. The second half of the claim is our own inference: "cannot apply to Adani group companies" and "clearest documented evidence that the regime is built around promoter-linked risk generically, not Adani by name". The circular never names Adani. That makes it analytic, not reported. It also overreaches, because the exclusion hits nearly every promoter-led group and so does not discriminate.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Replace srcs on c022 and on entity cap:sebi-mar2024-exemption with the primary record ["SEBI — Amendment to Circular for mandating additional disclosures by FPIs that fulfil certain objective criteria (Mar 2024)", "https://www.sebi.gov.in/legal/circulars/mar-2024/amendment-to-circular-for-mandating-additional-disclosures-by-fpis-that-fulfil-certain-objective-criteria_82418.html"]. verdicts.dateTest: The claim is: Hindenburg alleged on 10 Aug 2024 that the Buchs held a stake in IPE Plus Fund 1, made in 2015. That checks out. The archived Hindenburg report (web.archive.org of hindenburgresearch.com/sebi-chair-conflicts/) says "Published on August 10, 2024" and "Madhabi Buch and her husband Dhaval Buch first appear to have opened their account with IPE Plus Fund 1 on June 5th, 2015 in Singapore". verdicts.identityTest: The person is right: Madhabi Puri Buch, SEBI Chairperson Mar 2022 to Feb 2025, with spouse Dhaval Buch. The fund is right: Hindenburg names it "GDOF Cell 90 (IPEplus Fund 1)", a Mauritius-registered cell below the Bermuda Global Dynamic Opportunities Fund, managed by IIFL (now 360 ONE). No LEI, CIN or registration number is recorded for the fund node, and none is available from these sources. The phrase "tied to a Vinod Adani associate" misstates what Hindenburg said. The report says a "Vinod Adani controlled company had invested in GDOF ... which then invested in IPE Plus Fund 1", meaning Vinod Adani himself used the structure. It says the fund's founder and CIO, Anil Ahuja, "was a director of Adani Enterprises ... three terms spanning nine years ending in June 2017". Its summary line is "run by an Adani director and significantly used by Vinod Adani".
verdicts.baseRate: Not computable. There is no public dataset of SEBI members' pre-appointment offshore holdings. As the file's own void notes, no public recusal or conflict-of-interest register existed before the 2025 High-Level Committee. What would make the claim stand out is that the fund was small (US$38.43m AUM at Dec 2017, per Hindenburg citing IIFL) and shared a structure with a Vinod Adani entity. That cannot be benchmarked against other regulators' holdings. Symmetry: an identical fields check on other SEBI members or earlier chairs is impossible for the same reason (no register). This lens does not frame a family, religion or ethnicity as the actor. The actor is a named individual office-holder, and Vinod Adani is a named individual.
verdicts.denialFound: Yes. The Buchs issued a joint statement on 11 Aug 2024, carried by NewsOnAir (same URL as the cited source): "the allegations are untrue and that their life and finances are an open book ... all disclosures as required have already been furnished to SEBI over the years"; "The alleged investments reportedly date back to 2015, well before Madhabi Buch's appointment as a full-time member of SEBI in 2017". This is already recorded as contra c027. There were further, widely reported points: the fund CIO Anil Ahuja was Dhaval Buch's childhood friend, the fund never invested in Adani securities, and 360 ONE WAM said the Buchs' investment was under 1.5% of fund inflows and the fund held no Adani shares. I remember these but did not re-fetch them in this pass (search budget exhausted), so they should be sourced before being added. Separately, the Lokpal dismissed the related complaints on 28 May 2025 (c028).
verdicts.innocentReading: A couple of private citizens living in Singapore in 2015 invested salary money in a small IIFL-managed offshore fund because its CIO was a family friend. They did this two years before she held any regulatory office. The fund's other investors, including a Vinod Adani entity, had nothing to do with their choice. Required disclosures were made to SEBI on appointment, and the units were redeemed in 2018. Under this reading, sharing a fund vehicle with Vinod Adani's entity is a coincidence of the same manager and structure, not a conflict. It stays open whether any recusal on Adani matters followed, because no recusal log has been published.
verdicts.reason: The core claim holds against the primary document. The archived Hindenburg report of 10 Aug 2024 does allege "hidden stakes" in IPE Plus Fund 1, with the account opened on 5 Jun 2015, so "alleged" is the right tier for the "undisclosed" part. The Buchs' own statement admits the 2015 investment, so the existence of the holding is effectively conceded. It is the "hidden/undisclosed" part and the alleged conflict that remain disputed. The claim is not refuted, but the record has specific errors. (1) The only cited source (NewsOnAir) says just "owned stakes in offshore entities linked to the Adani Group" and 2015. It does not name IPE Plus Fund 1, Mauritius or Vinod Adani, so the source check is partial and the primary report must be added. (2) "Vinod Adani associate" misstates the allegation: Hindenburg says Vinod Adani himself used the structure and the fund was run by an Adani director (Anil Ahuja). (3) The record's d says the stake size was not stated in the report, which is false: Hindenburg gives US$872,762.25 per a 26 Feb 2018 account statement. (4) The own-edge dates show the allegation date, not the ownership window. (5) supersededBy c028 is wrong, because the Lokpal dismissal of corruption complaints does not supersede the allegation that the stake existed.
verdicts.corrections:
1. srcs: add the primary source, Hindenburg Research, "Whistleblower Documents Reveal SEBI's Chairperson Had Stake In Obscure Offshore Entities Used In Adani Money Siphoning Scandal", 10 Aug 2024, via the web.archive.org copy of https://hindenburgresearch.com/sebi-chair-conflicts/ (the live site returns 404). Keep NewsOnAir only as the source for the denial.
2. text/lab/d and the entity node's d: change "tied to a Vinod Adani associate" / "used by an associate of Vinod Adani" to "a fund Hindenburg said was used, via the Bermuda GDOF, by a Vinod Adani-controlled company, and whose founder and CIO Anil Ahuja was an Adani Enterprises director until June 2017".
3. d: delete "Stake size not disclosed in the report ... amount not stated". Replace it with "Hindenburg: total value US$872,762.25 per account statement dated 26 Feb 2018 (whistleblower documents); % of fund not stated by Hindenburg." Set `a` to about ₹ crore only if converted with the date and rate stated, otherwise leave null.
4. from/to: set from=2015-06-05 and to=2018 (redemption requested 25 Feb 2018 per Hindenburg). Record the 2024-08-10 allegation date in d, not as the ownership window.
5. d: add that the holding overlapped her WTM tenure (Apr 2017 to Feb 2018 redemption request) and the 22 Mar 2017 transfer of account authority to Dhaval Buch, both flagged as per Hindenburg.
6. Remove supersededBy "rules-regulators:c028", or reclassify it as a related contra. The Lokpal order dismissed corruption complaints and did not rule on whether the stake existed or was disclosed.
7. Split the edge: the existence of the 2015 holding is admitted by the Buchs' statement (a party admission, so it can be tiered higher). The "undisclosed" and conflict-of-interest parts stay alleged, with contra c027.
